speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 29.	That with the approval of the governor in council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Mines and Resources there be allowed a tax credit of fifty per centum of expenditures incurred by a corporation, asoeiation or syndicate or exploration partnership whose principal business is the production, refining or marketing of petroleum or the exploration or drilling for oil, on a well spudded in between June 26, 1944, and March 31, 1945, which proves to be unproductive, provided that such well is a deep-test well the drilling of which is deemed desirable in the interest of extending the petroleum resources of Canada and which could not reasonably have been expected to be undertaken without such tax credit.

Under this resolution a tax credit of fifty per cent is to be allowed on exploration work and drilling for oil. The section of the country from which I come contains a considerable natural gas industry. The Minister of National Revenue will know something about this because many homes in Hamilton are heated with gas. A good deal of exploration work is being done by this industry. Has consideration been given to extending this privilege to exploration work for natural gas as well as for oil?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I can give a word of explanation as to the purpose of this section. As the minister said in his budget speech, the purpose of the resolution is as follows:
It is, I think, in the national interest that some -additional encouragement be offered to the Canadian oil industry to undertake the drilling of several deep-test wells in certain areas with a view to proving up significant, geological structures.
At present, as the committee is aware, tax credits are allowed in respect of unproductive wildcat wells. These tax credits are'equivalent to the -writing off of this expenditure as an expense in profit and loss account, The present provision is somewhat more generous in the benefits to be allowed. It should be emphasized that this special tax credit is allowed only in respect of projects approved by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Mines and Resources, and will apply only in cases where it could not reasonably have been expected that the project would be undertaken without special assistance. In other words it is to encourage operators to drill in non-proven areas where our government geologists would like to see deep-test wells drilled in order to determine whether or not the area is oil bearing. For that reason, on projects approved by the Minister of Mines and Resources and authorized by order in council the special tax credit will be given. As the committee will appreciate, the effect of this will be that the oil explorer gambles fifty cents of his own 
money and the government says, "If you will do that, we will give you a tax credit of fifty cents on the dollar."

I would like to know why you do not give one hundred per cent on the cost of drilling oil wells that do not materialize. In the Dawson Creek area, in the Pouce Coupe area, in British Columbia, in the Peace River area in Alberta, in southwestern Saskatchewan, in northeastern Alberta south of the Saskatchewan -river, legitimate oil people have been drilling for oil. These wells cost up to $150,000 -and more. I observed these men working and I know the difficulties under which they labour. If oil were found it would be a wonderful thing for the country; why should we not allow all the cost of a well that does not produce anything?
The people I have in mind are not wildcatters; they are legitimate oil -producers. For instance, Imperial Oil of Turner Valley are operating. I do not know whether they would be entitled to consideration, but I did see a number of wells that had been drilled in the Turner valley and which have not produced anything. Why should not the producers of such wells be given some consideration in the way of taxation?
No country needs oil production more than Canada. We are producing now about 12,000,000 barrels a year and are using from 80,000,000 to 100,000,000 barrels a year, speaking from memory. Canada would be in jeopardy if her oil supplies from outside were cut off. While no doubt this fifty per cent allowance will be acceptable to the legitimate oil companies, I do not see why they should not be allowed one hundred per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is no doubt aware, the tax structure does allow substantial tax credits to companies drilling wildcat wells or for off-property drilling. Section 8, subsection 6, reads as follows:
A corporation whose principal business is the production and/or refining and/or marketing of petroleum and/or petroleum products shall be entitled in respect of the year of expenditure to deduct from the sum total of the income tax payable by it under this act and the tax payable under -the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, (and if such sum -total of tax is not sufficient to provide therefor, to deduct any balance from the -tax of subsequent years) forty per centum of
(a)	all drilling costs incurred by it directly or indirectly on oil wells -spudded in during the period from the first day of January, 1943. to -the -thirty-first day of March, 1945, and abandoned within six months after completion of such drilling; and
(b)	all exploration costs, including -all general geological and geophysical expenses incurred by it:

Income TFar Tax
provided, however, that in the case of a corporation substantially all of whose income is subject to depletion under the provisions oi this act, the deduction to be allowed hereunder shall he twenty-six and two-thirds per centum of such costs instead of forty per centum.
As I indicated a moment ago, this is a special type of drilling, and the tax credit is granted because it is believed _ that these people would not engage in this type of drilling if they were not given special encouragement. But if we were to give them their entire costs it seems to me it would be pretty much a case of heads I win and tails you lose as far as the oil company was concerned. They would get a tax credit for the entire cost of drilling the well, and if anything should develop they would get the benefit. It is felt that while this is not excessive, it is a reasonable inducement to offer for a special type of drilling on projects which are approved by the Minister of Mines and Resources and authorized by order in council.

During my last visit to Turner valley I spent some time watching the drilling of a deep well. I have forgotten just how deep it was, but I know they were using a large-sized pipe, and it runs through my head that the operator told me the well would cost perhaps half a million dollars. Right there the question of tax allowance came up.
The Imperial Oil is a reputable company; there are other companies in Canada just as good, but none better. The parliamentary assistant spoke a moment ago about an allowance of fifty per cent being made, which would be sufficient perhaps to prevent unnecessary drilling. The Imperial Oil company, a corporation of that magnitude, with their experience, with the geologists and the equipment they have to enable them to ascertain whether oil is below, would not likely drill anywhere unless all the indications pointed to the presence of oil. They have put, I suppose, half a million dollars in the well which I saw-my recollection is that the well would cost about that-and if nothing comes out of it the Imperial Oil cannot make anything out of it, yet if the well should produce oil the whole of Canada would profit from it. I suggest the utmost consideration as far as taxation is concerned should be extended in a case of that kind.
I called to see another area out west of Nordegg. in northern Alberta, away west of Rocky Mountain House, on the north Saskatchewan river. There were a number of men with equipment drilling for oil. If they do not find oil there, of course the cost will be an investment cost to the Imperial Oil.
But there again it seems to me that in any honest-to-goodness effort to discover oil, consideration by way of tax relief should be given to any reputable company which makes a real effort in this direction. The Imperial Oil is a well-known company which has done a very great deal for this country.

This resolution proposes to give a tax credit to corporations, and I notice that the next one proposes that it shall be given in respect of strategic minerals. I wonder whether the minister has considered the possibility of regarding oil as a strategic mineral, in view of the great need for it which exists at the present time, and thus making it possible for tire individual investor under certain conditions to get a tax credit for the amount he contributes towards the drilling of an oil well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This resolution, as my hon. friend will have seen, applies not only to corporations but to associations, syndicates or exploration partnerships.
But not to individuals?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: But not to individuals. I do not know whether there are individuals engaging in these deep test wells, but the expenditure would be so considerable that it is unlikely, I should think, that any one man would do that. This benefit is available to partnerships for instance.

That is the money which is made by the partnership? Suppose a number of men group together and each contributes so many thousands of dollars to the drilling of a well, can each individual taxpayer get a tax credit in that case?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, under our taxation system, as the hon. member knows, we do not tax the syndicate or partnership as such. We tax the individual partners. So that the tax credit would be applied, I take it, by the individual partners in proportion to their interests in the syndicate or partnership.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
30. That the tax credit allowed to a taxpayer of forty per centum of contributions made by him in the year 1943 to associations, syndicates or mining partnerships organized for the purpose of prospecting in Canada for base metals or strategic minerals be extended to include a tax credit in respect of contributions in the year 1944.
I think that the purpose of this clause is to extend to 1944 the assistance which was given in 1943; is not that so?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is correct.

Income War Tax

But I do not think that that assistance was open to the prospector or to the individual who so frequently uses his money to grubstake a 'prospector. In the southern part of British Columbia those great rugged mountain areas have been worked over in the past by, shall I term- him, the old-fashioned prospector. But now, what with tuition by mining classes given by the provinces, another class of prospector has arisen who is capable of making use of modern experience and modern instruments, and there is a very great need for the whole of that area to be explored again by geological exploration. It is quite true that at the present time labour is scarce and that individuals are not so able to use their money for the purpose of grubstaking as they were; but the time will shortly arrive when there will be great opportunities of going back to the old method, so common in British Columbia, of individuals putting their money up to back a prospector.
Reference has already been made in this house to the words of advice given us by a member of the geological survey of Canada, drawing attention to the fact that not more than five per cent of the great north country is now properly geologically explored; drawing attention also to the fact that, of the great producing mines of to-day, hardly more than one of them have been discovered in this generation. So that our object should be to do everything we possibly can to further exploration, and for that purpose we need the prospector.
In the working over of the mountains in the southern part of my constituency mines have been discovered, most interesting prospects have been discovered. Copper is mined, platinum has been taken from the creeks, gold and silver are mined, and over a huge area there are valuable showings of lead and zinc. I want to keep going the old method, the old habit, of having the money of individuals used to back the prospector to work over that whole area again, in the hope that mines so far not discovered may yet be discovered. Will the parliamentary assistant tell us whether there is any possibility of extending this facility to the individual who risks his money in that way, not by investing it in a company whose business is prospecting, but investing it in a way which will enable the individual prospector to go out and do the work?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am afraid there is very
little prospect of this being extended to the individual prospector. As my hon. friend will realize, in a sense this is a rather loose section; it is a straight tax credit to a contribution or

an investment which is made to a prospecting syndicate, association or partnership. That was pretty carefully considered last year when the section was originally brought in, and after consideration it was felt that, in view of the very loose nature of the section, of necessity it should not be extended to cover payments made the individual prospector. This resolution merely extends for another year the incentive legislation put in last year. I can bring my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the minister, but frankly I feel there is little or no possibility of his being prepared to extend that concession.
But why was the section made so loose?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The looseness is not so much in the section as it is in the description of the groups to which a contribution may be made. My own view on this matter is this. I have always had rather serious doubts of the desirability of this legislation-as I say, this is only my personal view-because it gave a very great incentive to stock promoters to [DOT] organize these prospecting syndicates and sell shares on the basis of getting the tax deduction. But weighing one thing against another, the desirability of encouraging prospecting and so on, it was felt that this concession should be made. To extend it beyond registered or incorporated prospecting companies or syndicates to individuals was going further than the government felt it should. Perhaps that decision was wrong, but I do not think it is likely to be changed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I crave the indulgence of the committee for a few moments while I discuss the subject before the chair in my capacity as an ordinary member. I have been greatly honoured by my appointment to the chair, and have fully enjoyed the cooperation that I have received from everyone. But as I represent a very populous and widespread constituency with diversified interests, and more particularly with gold mining as one of the predominant industries, I should like to say a few words on the item under discussion. I am entirely in agreement with the present resolution the purpose of which is to help base and other metals, but I am at a loss to understand why gold is not included.
I do not wish to precipitate a controversy over this subject, because my position rather precludes anything of the sort; but at times gold mining has been maligned, notwithstanding the fact that it has played a very important part in the economic life of the nation for at least the last thirty years. I am in a position to know what I am speaking about in this regard because I represent great pro-

Income War Tax
ducers in the Porcupine section and1 I am a neighbour to the Kirkland Lake section in Ontario on the one hand and the Noranda-Rouyn-Val d'Or district on the Quebec side, on the other. I have first-hand knowledge and personal experience of what has been accomplished by the gold mining industry throughout that district and of the contribution it has made to the national and particularly the economic life of the country.
It was certainly marvellous, during the depression, to see what was being done by those sections of the country to give full employment to Canadians. Not only did the miners themselves enjoy the benefit of the employment provided, but agriculture also benefited and the forest activities consequent upon gold mining were promoted.
We knew from the experience of 1914-1918 that gold mining would be a war victim, so that in the fall of 1939 and early in 1940 we anticipated what would follow. But when the government made an appeal to the industry for increased production in order to maintain the Canadian dollar and our balance of export trade with the United States, both the management and the miners themselves responded magnificently. Since those days, however, very grave things have happened and both the *management and the men have been willing to cooperate with the government to the fullest possible extent. They do not want hand-outs. They are anxious to play fair with the people and to pay their full share of taxation. They are not going to ask for favours from this government or from any provincial administration. All they want is fair consideration of their problems. Two years ago the town of Timmins, the whole of the Porcupine district including Schumacher, South Porcupine, the Kirkland Lake section and the Noranda district, sent a delegation here who presented a very able brief to the government, eloquently delivered by Mr. T. R. Langdon, urging the importance of maintaining at least a skeleton force to exploit the gold mining industry. They pointed out that if this were not done a great many people would suffer from the resulting lack of development, more particularly the municipal bodies. They pointed out further the excellent work carried on through the agency of these gold mining operations. They received a fine response from the Minister of Finance who was much impressed by the representations made, and many of the grievances complained of were remedied.
The mineral resources of Canada, generally speaking, belong to the provinces. It is true that outside the northwestern terirtory the mines in this country belong to the various provinces, but it must be remembered that 100-317i
ninety-one per cent of the taxation which they
pay goes to the federal treasury, and that fact alone must make the federal treasury realize that under such conditions certain anomalies-
I will not call them injustices-exist in connection with gold mining in some of the provinces. We must keep the record straight. The central government has responsibilities in this matter. If we plot the gross value of Canada's mineral production for, let us say, ten years back, and then project the curve let us say five years into the future, the trend will startle us, and I think it will be readily admitted that a drastic or radical charge could not be regarded as premature, as has been stated in the House of Commons. I am not discussing the question of the gold standard or of monetary systems, but I suggest that if we try to visualize the conditions that are to prevail in the future, we shall see that the gold standard will have to be maintained after the war, and for this reason Canada is in a fortunate position in that it is one of the large gold producing countries in the world. If gold mining has meant a great deal to Canada in the past, it will mean a great deal to the future of this dominion, and I am sure it will play an important part in the post-war period.
I have no quarrel with anything that is done to promote the development of base metals, but surely it should be found possible to include gold mining in any programme that is implemented by the federal government. New oil and gold mining companies were given a three-year tax exemption. On the surface this is a real concession, but when in practice it is discovered that during that three-year period it is necessary to write off depreciation and pre-development costs at a fixed rate per annum, the picture changes. In practice, experience has taught that the concession has no real or worth-while value. I leave that thought with hon. members to think over. I do not expect that drastic changes will be made at once, but I hope that these representations which I am now making will be taken into consideration.
It is true that last year the cost of outside exploration for base or strategic minerals was allowed as a deductible item, but such expenditures were limited to something like $5,000. This is a feeble and hesitating step in the right direction, but why limit it to base and strategic metals? Why not include gold? I am not theorizing on that score, because I have first-hand knowledge of the situation, and I have seen what it has meant to this country to have had gold mining operations in Canada. I know what it has meant to my own section of the country and to the rest
Income War Tax

of Canada. Those engaged in gold mining are willing now, as they have been in the past, to make a one hundred per cent contribution to the development of Canada and to its war effort, provincially and federally. But some people seem to think that mining operations can be enlarged or curtailed at will on short notice. There seems to be no understanding of the fact that it takes four or five years, frequently longer, to bring a gold prospect into profitable production, and that in order to obtain that one profitable development it is necessary to weed out a large number of losing ventures for which no provision is made in the mine tax structure. If we are to play any real part in providing post war employment, we may be somewhat late now in anything we do in connection with gold mining.
Many people regard gold mining as a sort of luscious bonanza. Some people seem to think it is like some fruit that grows in abundance and has only to be picked. Well, it may surprise the committee to learn that out of 4,500 ventures, only two per cent come to full development and that only one per cent of gold mining ventures have been paying dividends. It can readily be seen, when you take these facts into consideration, that gold mining presents us with a serious problem. It would be easy to single out one or two or three mines in my own constituency which are paying dividends, but I know of hundreds of mortalities among the new projects-ventures which never come to fruition at all. It is interesting to note the concern that is felt for the oil industry as well as for the base metals, which have their raison d'etre.
We must also realize that it is almost impossible to differentiate between gold mining and the mining industry generally under present conditions. Let us for one brief moment look at the mining industry generally, not gold mining only, which means so much to our national economy. We will take as an example the boot and shoe industry. No doubt there are different factors connected with that industry compared with mining generally, but the raw material is always easy to obtain in Canada, United States or Great Britain. We may send government agencies outside of Canada to sell the products of the boot and shoe industry. This industry has a large national market. You cannot apply the same principles to gold mining or mining generally, because it employs practically only two factors. The first is the size and grade of the ore deposits, and the other the cost of production. That applies more forcibly to gold mining than to any other mining in Canada, because in 
most cases they are mining a very low grade of ore indeed. This applies particularly to the old mines. No doubt a lot of new mines will come into operation after the war as they did when the United States increased the price of gold to $35 an ounce, if proper attention to its problems are given. The new price did much more than that; it gave a much longer life to some of the old producers that had been producing for a number of years.
As I say, the second factor is the cost of production. That must necessarily enter into gold mining as it does in any other kind of mining industry in this country. For industry generally there has been set up a standard profit based upon a fixed standard period. Anything over that standard profit is subject to a so-called hundred per cent excess profits tax, but for industry other than gold mining any profits equal to-and I wish the committee to pay particular attention to this-or less than the computed standard profits are not subject to the hundred per cent excess profits tax.
To encourage gold production in the early stages of the war, the gold mines, you will remember, were urged to increase gold production by every possible means. Hon. members will be familiar with that situation. To encourage the increased production of gold it was arranged that the' standard profit base should move up with the increase in production measured in ounces of gold. In other words, if a mining company doubled its ounces produced, its standard profit base would be doubled. Then, to punish those who might remain indifferent to the government's appeal, it was further arranged that where the ounces produced fell below the output during the standard period, the standard profit base would diminish in the same ratio. At the time the industry raised no objection to this arrangement; but conditions changed. The government declared gold mining non-essential and placed it in the lowest category. I know the government will realize there was no protest from any of the gold mines or from any of the workers in this section either because we knew there was a war on and we were absolutely in favour of a total war effort. However, increased production was not allowed to continue, and decreased production could not be avoided. As a result, gold mines are now discriminated against. The boot and shoe company, as an example, can make up to the standard base before the hundred per cent excess profits tax is applicable, but not so the gold mines. To show the unfairness of this situation, let us assume that a producer in my section ceases all mining operations and

Income War Tax
that after paying the cost of maintenance they have out of their return from their investments sufficient income to cover costs and retain a small margin. No matter how small that margin is, it is excess profits subject to a hundred per cent levy, because no gold is being produced. There can be no difference of opinion as to whether or not such an arrangement is equitable and just.
I wish to mention one other matter which is very important. Proven and potential ore reserves constitute the mine's real assets, and from the moment abstraction begins, the sum total of these assets is being diminished. It is a wasting asset, different from agriculture or some other industry. That applies to gold mining in every section of the world. In a comparatively short time these assets are completely liquidated. It follows then that the earning power of a gold mine is comparatively brief and very largely unpredictable, and cannot be treated by the intelligent investor as a selfiperpetuating industry such as an ordinary commercial or industrial enterprise.
The committee no doubt will be surprised to learn that if to-morrow I were to invest in some of the old producers in my section like Hollinger, MacIntyre and Dome at the present day prices and the company never reduced or missed the dividend paid at the present time, it would take over eighty-three years to get my capital back without interest.
I thank the committee for its kind indulgence in allowing me to bring to its attention some of the difficulties of gold mining. In making this appeal I make it in an open-minded way, realizing that the industry has done much for our national economy in the past as it is bound to be called upon to do in the future. I also make it on behalf of the miners themselves, who have been fruitfully employed for the last thirty years in my own section of the county. They have meant a lot to the economy of Canada. The man-power situation in that section is now tight, because nobody backslided so far as voluntary enlistments were concerned. I am making the appeal in behalf of the farmers in my section of the country. The new clay belt was opened up over thirty years ago. The success of the farmers in that section largely depended on the success of the -mining centres. I am making my appeal sincerely, not only in the name of my own constituency but in behalf of the people of the whole of Canada, and more particularly from the point of view of the great help that the gold mining industry is -bound to be called upon to give in the post-war period. *

Under the resolution as it stands a tax credit is allowed to a taxpayer up to forty per cent of contributions made -by him to associations, syndicates, mining partnerships organized for the purpose of prospecting in Canada for base metals, and so on. I think the provsion is too narrow. Contributions made by a taxpayer to individual prospectors should receive the same proportion of tax credit. On June 7 I wrote the Minister of Finance suggesting to him that a taxpayer in Canada contributing to prospectors for base or strategic metals should be entitled to deduct from the income tax payable by him under the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act of 1940 an amount equal to forty per cent of the contribution so made by him, as is allowed- to taxpayers who contribute to associations, syndicates or mining partnerships registered or otherwise recognized by the laws of any province of Canada, and as provided and regulated by section 8, subsections 4 and 5, of the Income War Tax Act. I suggested to him that any -prospector or prospecting partnership in Canada should register their activities with the mining recorder on payment of a fee and file with the mining recorder a sworn statement of work done and amounts so expended, such statement to be filed by the mining recorder with the inspector of income tax, and upon making return for income tax such taxpayer should file a similar sworn statement with corroborating evidence, with the inspector of income tax. I said further to the minister:
I know that it is common -practice for people living in Yukon and British Columbia -and I dare say in other provinces to advance money to prospectors, so making it possible for them to remain in the field and to carry on prospecting. I have frequently done so myself -but not since such contributions have been dealt with in tax legislation.
It would seem only just that bona fide contributions so made and proved by individuals should be similarly exempt -as contributions made to associations, syndicates or mining partnerships and I respectfully request that the proposal be given your favourable consideration and be appropriately dealt with in the coming budget and attendant legislation.	.
To that letter the minister replied ou June 28 as follows:
As you know-, my colleague the Minister of National Revenue is charged with the administration and -interpretation of tax legislation. Whether, from his point of view, your suggestion would be practicable I cannot say. However, I am forwarding a copy of your letter to him for consideration, and I shall be pleased to discuss the point with -him when this item is_ being considered in connection with the new income tax amendments which will shortly be before the house.
I hope the minister has been as good as his word and has discussed the matter with the
Income War Tax

Minister of National Revenue, and that between them they will agree to a broadening of this provision to allow the same credit to a taxpayer for contributions made by him to an individual prospector, registered and properly approved, as is now allowed for contributions to associations, syndicates and mining partnerships. It is only fair to do this. .

The key word of this resolution, it seems to me, as with the resolution of last year, is "prospecting". The government decided that it was wise to encourage pros-' pecting in Canada, and there can be no doubt whatever as to the soundness of that decision. The whole mining industry depends upon new mines being found. For some few years now comparatively few have been discovered in Canada. I think the government was quite right in taking the step that was taken last year, in providing for this tax credit. At that time some of us suggested that it should be extended to include the individual prospector, and certainly the time has now come when that should be done. From my own knowledge of the situation in British Columbia I can say that the great majority of the .mines there were discovered by individual prospectors who went out in the hope of striking something worth while. They were found as the result of individual initiative. That is quite a different matter from having men sent out by big companies, but under the present arrangement the companies are the ones who are helped. Most of the mines in British Columbia were found by men who went out on their own, in many cases backed by the local merchant or someone else in the town in which they lived. We feel very deeply about this matter in British Columbia, because we are convinced that the only way we will find new mines is by having individual prospectors go out once more, just as they went out at the turn of the century. The British Columbia-Yukon chamber of mines have made representations along this line. I have here a wire in which they say:
We also urge that tax deductions of contributions for prospecting at present granted persons financing associations, syndicates or mining partnerships be extended to include individual prospectors financing themselves.
The position is that the government is helping the big fellow but is not helping the little fellow. That is exactly what it amounts to. I do not object to the help being given the mining companies or syndicates, but I say it is far more important to help the prospector and his friend in the town who is willing to put up money so that the prospector may carry on his work. We are going to have several hundred thousand young men coming

back from the armed forces one of these days, perhaps before the next budget is considered, and I am convinced that many of them would take up mining and go out prospecting if they were given reasonable encouragement. A measure such as we are suggesting, that is the extension of this tax credit to cover individual cases, would be one way to help those young returned men get into the hills and take up prospecting. They are just the right age, just the right type. They are the finest young men in Canada, young men of great initiative, and I am convinced that they could do something really worth while for the mining industry if the governments of this country, not only the federal government but also the provincial governments, gave them reasonable encouragement. We realize that there would be difficulties in working out these tax credits in connection with individuals; perhaps that is why it has not been done so far. The government cannot work out a method of doing it; it is just too much trouble to try. It is a comparatively easy matter in connection with the big companies, but when it comes to helping the little fellow they just do not know how to go about it and therefore they say he cannot be helped. This matter should not be simply pushed aside. The government should take some steps to give this assistance, under this budget, to the individual prospector.

I want to say a few words on this item, and first I would state that I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South. I think he made a very important point. To follow that through, however, after the individual prospector or whoever may grubstake him is given a tax credit, under present arrangements any discovery he may make is handed over to some private company to exploit. In this field, particularly in the post-war period, if the government is going to invest money in the discovery and development of new mineral resources; if the taxpayers of Canada are to foot the bill through tax credits and so on, at least they should get something in return by way of social services. I am a little doubtful as to whether that is practical on this item. Up to the present I think this was a practical arrangement made necessary because of the urgency of the war situation. I believe the government had to take the position of helping everyone who might find and develop base metal mines; the urgency of the war made that necessary. At the present time, however, I think our war requirements are being fairly well met, so I think now we should carefully examine the situation and lay down certain regulations to

Income War Tax
cover future developments in connection with any operation in base metals. We should take great care to see that they are so located as to fit into the economy of this country, and have some peace-time usefulness when the war is over.

How can
you affect their location? They are where nature left them.

I will give an example of what is happening now, and will leave it to hon. members to decide whether this is a profitable investment for the people of Canada to make. I had a visit from some of the employees of the Quyon Molybdenite company, located not far from here. This company began operations in 1940; it was a war-time set-up. In addition to other assistance they were given a subsidy of 75 cents a pound on the metal they produced. Later that subsidy was discontinued, and the company immediately ceased operations. The plant was taken over by another company, headed by Mr. J. E. Gray of Toronto, who operated it until a week or so ago. The employees of that company have not been paid since June 15. That company was largely the creation of the federal government, and continued in operation only as long as that operation was profitable. You see, the war does not enter into the picture as far as these people are con-concerned. As long as it was profitable, as long as they were subsidized, as long as they were making money out of it, it was fine and they were prepared to stay. That is the sort of private enterprise about which the hon. member for York-Sunbury talks.
Oh, you are just talking sheer nonsense.

I have the floor, Mr. Chairman. All morning I listened to my hon. friends to my right talking about private enterprise-private enterprise with both arms round the neck of the government. They say, "We will go as far as the government is prepared to finance us, but when that financing is not forthcoming we will walk out." The point I am making is this. While you are protecting the fellow who wishes to make money, at the same time you are building up a community on that basis, as happened in this instance. Employees were working for this company. It was a new set-up, and they moved in, taking their families with them. Some established homes. They have an investment and an equity in that community which was not government subsidized. If the regulations are such that just as soon as a fellow cannot make money he can pull up, walk out and leave the
property completely valueless, then I say the employees or the people in the community are entitled to some protection. There should be some understanding that organizations subsidized by the government into new industry owe some responsibility to the community. It should be pointed out to them that they cannot just walk out without even paying wages. Let us remember that the average worker depends from week to week on his daily wage. They have received no wages since June 15, and they are frozen to their jobs because they are in a high priority industry. Selective service has not allowed them to move out to other employment.
I thought it was closed down.
If it was closed they could move out.

They have not, so far. I am not arguing about selective service, because I think that end of the matter will be taken care of, once it is understood. The point I am making is that this has been an attempt to establish a new industry to produce base metals for war purposes. We must now concern ourselves with this situation: If the government is going to give tax concessions to those who want to establish industry, then it is the responsibility of the government to see to it that regardless of where mineral deposits are found, if we are going to spend money we should have a permanent industry, and one which can be routed into our peace-time economy. Let us assure ourselves that it will not be just a mushroom growth for the purpose of making money during the war, and that those in charge will not be able to walk out and leave it.
The hon. member said it was still working.
No, it is not still working. The workers are trying to put a lien against the property for their wages.
The hon. member said that selective service would not let them get jobs elsewhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have been listening to what the hon. member has been saying, and while I do not like to rise to a point of order, still I must point out that the subject he is discussing is a long way from that of concessions to prospectors. I wish my hon. friend would try to bring his remarks within the resolution.

I think I am absolutely within it; I am on the point. I have shown what has happened, something that the government
Income War Tax

is apparently going to continue. I am urging that some regard should be had by the government to the establishment of base metal industries, so that it may preclude what is taking place now, namely exploitation for war purposes. This is a use of the taxpayers' money, and when it is no longer profitable, or when the government is not prepared to continue to make it a paying proposition, out of the public treasury, private enterprise picks up and walks out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The question whether or not the government should subsidize an unprofitable industry is away outside the provisions of this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word, although I am not going into the ramifications of the position outlined by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I do not know much about molybdenite, but I understand the great production is in the United States. Someone discovered some of it in Canada and thought it would help the war efiort. The government gave a subsidy. I suppose it was found unprofitable, and the subsidy was withdrawn. Someone with private initiative thought he would stake something or risk something, and he failed and folded up. I suggest the plight of the men is bad, but they have their remedy against the directors of the company. I am sorry for them, and I would do anything I could to help them; but it is not at all germane to the subject matter we are now discussing.
I should like to add a word in support of the plea made by my three colleagues from the west coast-the hon. member for Yale, the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Vancouver South. On principle, if it is right to give a tax concession to a company or to a syndicate which sends out its employees, finances them and reaps the profit of their knowledge and industry- probably out of all proportion to what a private individual would do for and reap from prospectors-then on principle it is right that this same assistance should be extended to two private individuals, one the prospector and the other the man who grubstakes him.
The hon. member for Vancouver South has pointed out that it is the history of the industry that individual prospectors have discovered the most and the best mines. That ought to be encouraged. What have we here? We have here discrimination between two positions, and the reason is quite clear. In my vierw the reason is that in the case of a corporation or a syndicate, supervision or checking can easily be carried out and the

quantum of allowance determined with mathematical accuracy, while in the case of the individual it may be difficult. Obviously that is why there is a distinction and discrimination, because in my opinion the principle is absolutely the same. In fact if there is a weight, on balance, it is in favour of the individual prospector. I suggest that in respect of the Yukon, the hon. member for Yukon has given with great particularity the modus operandi which would protect the public treasury against fraud. It can be done in any individual case by the exercise of diligence and labour on the part of the taxing authorities. The difficulty is in administration, and I think the minister will tell us that when he comes to reply. I do suggest that in setting up the income tax too much regard is given to the convenience of administration, the centralization of administration, and not enough is given to business and employees of business. The whole thing is based upon this principle: how can we get the most dollars in the easiest possible way and with the least administrative difficulty? That is an indictment against the administrative policy of the department.
It is of course only natural that a departmental head would say, "Well, this is the easiest way; we can get the same results along an easier path." But they do not think the thing through clearly. They do not ask themselves: which is the better way, having regard to the whole national economy, and the public interest? I suggest the whole position ought to be reviewed. I am wondering if we have not put our finger right on the weakness of the administrative position, namely that this is an administrative problem they have not tackled and do not wish to tackle. It stands to reason that if it is a good principle to give a tax concession to a company or a syndicate or a group, then certainly that principle is sound as it applies to an individual. You cannot get away from it; you cannot deny it. In this instance if there is to be discrimination it would be to the greater advantage of the national economy and would bring about a greater national productivity if such discrimination were in favour of the individual rather than the company.
My reading of history is that individuals with inventive minds or a flair for prospecting who are employed or sent out by companies never have reaped the part of the reward that was due to their industry; it is taken up by the company concerned. I know that is true of individual inventions which have been financed by companies. I know it is true in connection with chemical research.

Income War Tax
I have a clear recollection of a chemical engineer of a very high type who delighted doing work of this kind. He was in the employ of a company and of course in receipt of a good salary. He would not have been there if he had not been getting that salary. But he had capabilities, and he discovered something, and I regret to have to say that he did not reap where he had sown to the extent that he ought to. This type of tax legislation just puts a premium on what I have been talking about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not know that there
is much I can add to what I said in reply to the hon. member for Yale. It does not seem entirely clear from the remarks of some hon. members that individual prospectors do not get any benefit. Apparently they would not get any benefit even if the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South were adopted.
The minister's assistant is not right. The man who grubstaked the prospector would get a credit, but the prospector would also get a tax credit for his expenses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That has never been suggested before to my knowledge.
I suppose he would get it automatically.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I suppose he would get it
as expenses. This resolution is intended to benefit the man who puts in an amount not exceeding $500 in the case of one association or syndicate, and not exceeding $5,000 in the case of contributions made to all such associations or syndicates. The man who is in the S100,000 income bracket may grubstake prospectors up to $5,000 provided that they are properly registered and are recognized as a prospecting syndicate. In the case of individual prospectors I could get one to go into the field-I am told there are none out of work at the moment. It is not simply a question of administrative difficulty, it is a matter of knowing whether or not a man is a prospector.
If I wanted to give a fellow a nice holiday I could give him $500 to go up and look around northern Quebec. He could spend his time on the delightful lakes up there. Perhaps he could take a pick along or he might even register as a prospector, but the result is that I would get an income tax credit. That would be extremely difficult to check.
It is an administrative difficulty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is more than an administrative difficulty. I think the view was that
the government would not be justified in extending it to the individual. That was the position taken last year, and so far as I know there has not been any change.
That is not an answer.

The parliamentary assistant has referred to the individual prospector who might go up into northern Quebec or some other mining section and have a holiday. The taxpayer who contributes and gets a tax credit does not go out himself. The syndicate does not go out, nor does the mining partnership. It is the prospectors who go out, and they are just as apt to go on a holiday as the man referred to by the parliamentary assistant. You cannot keep track of the individual prospector any easier when he is working for an individual than you can when he is working for an association or syndicate. What has the Minister of National Revenue to say? The Minister of Finance said that he would discuss it with him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon has referred to the Minister of Finance passing to me a letter that had been sent to him concerning this matter. What the Minister of Finance was referring to me was the question under section 8, subsection 5, whereby an allowance is made for an association, syndicate or mining partnership registered or otherwise recognized under the laws of any province of Canada. The hon. member for Yukon brought up the fact that this does not extend to the territories, and he contended that they were just as much entitled to it as the provinces. That matter is being taken care of in the legislation this year, and this allowance will be extended to residents of the Yukon and other territories.
Do I understand that contributions made by taxpayers to individual prospectors will be taken as a credit?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is a matter of finance, not for national revenue.

It could be easily accomplished by amending the resolution by adding the words "to individual prospectors" after the figure "1943" in the second line. The resolution would then read:
That the tax credit allowed to a taxpayer of forty per centum of contributions made by him in the year 1943 to individual prospectors, to associations, syndicates or mining partnerships organized for the purpose of prospecting in Canada for base metals or strategic minerals be extended to include a tax credit in respect of contributions in the year 1944.
You could do it by the addition of three
words to the resolution.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no trouble about doing it if the government felt it was proper to do it as a matter of policy. I have been endeavouring to explain for some time, no ' doubt inadequately, that after considering the matter fully last year and again this year the government felt that it could not go that far.
For administrative reasons?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would not say for administrative reasons only.

The objection is for administrative reasons, but the amendment I have suggested would obviate those administrative difficulties. Now the tax allowance is made only in the case of contributions to prospectors who organize and incorporate a company.

Mr. Chairman, the observations of the previous speakers should bring forcibly to the attention of the government the importance of the prospector. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue have taken part in a discussion of this matter, but where is the Minister of Mines and Resources? He is the man who should be evolving a broad and comprehensive programme of mining development in this country. He knows the provinces in which mining is most active.
I cannot recall a single mining property in British Columbia which is not the result of the efforts of an individual prospector. The great Sullivan mine, which gives employment directly or indirectly to 100,000 people, such as railway men, machinery men, and other employees, was discovered by a prospector many years ago. The individual prospector was the basis of all mining organizations. The different companies raised the money; the government did not raise it. Individuals subscribed for shares in these companies and smelters were built; machinery was bought. All of this contributed to the development of mines, which in British Columbia at least have created the greatest prosperity that that province has known.
The average life of a mine is twenty years, and then comes the depletion period for which the mining industry is asking a fifty per cent depletion. After twenty years most mines have to close and unemployment is created. As one of the members noted, in the post-war period it is the mining industry that will create the most employment and the most prosperity. I do not know of any better argument I can present that the prospector is the basis of it all than to state the fact that in British Columbia, you can count seven smelters which have gone out of business, or rather,

seven smelters which have been treating British Columbia ores; one of them is on the international boundary. These smelters created an immense amount of business and a great volume of employment. Then we come to the gold mining industry. In 1938 there were thirty-nine plants in British Columbia for the treatment of gold ores. To-day there are just seven. There is no encouragement from the government. The department of mines should cooperate with the various provinces in a broad and comprehensive programme for the recreation of the mining interests and the mining activity and the mining development in every province which appeals to the prospector.

I want to go on record as supporting the contention of the hon. member for Kootenay West. The minister has a peculiar idea, and the Department of Finance has an even more peculiar idea, that this is a generous thing which they are doing. Let me say this: you limit it to base metals or strategic minerals. In the view of the treasury officials that is what they want. Now, base metals and strategic metals are frequently found in connection with mining gold. I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister that they reword this clause and omit the words "for base metals or strategic minerals.", and so have the section in this form:
That the -tax credit allowed to a taxpayer of forty per centum of contributions made by him in the year 1943 to associations, syndicates or mining partnerships organized for the purpose of prospecting in Canada shall be extended to include a tax credit in respect of contributions in the year 1944.
To apply to all metals.

To apply to all metals, to apply to all prospectors, because in our peculiar and very intricate geological structure, if you limit the prospector to going out looking for strategic or base metals you will find that the clause will have very little effect at the present time. It is of very little use to the prospector, because it is an extremely limiting clause. I believe we could well follow the Australian practice, by which they allow one hundred per cent as a deduction for prospecting, up to a certain percentage of the total income. I am going to read the specific clause, because I think it is important, particularly at this time in the war. Clause 23 provides:
The following income shall be exempt from income tax:

Income War Tax
That is, it is unequivocally exempt from income tax. Here is the clause concerning the prospector:
(p) Income derived by a tbona fide prospector from the sale, transfer or assignment by him of his rights to mine for gold in a particular area in Australia or in the territory of New Guinea. For the .purpose of this paragraph "bona fide prospector" means a person, other than a company, who has personally carried out the whole or major part of the field work of prospecting for gold in the particular area, or who has contributed to the expenditure incurred in the work of prospecting and development in that area, and includes a company which has itself carried out the whole or major part of such work.
That is a broad provision, and I think it is a sound and reasonable clause to insert at this time in our act. We are going into the postwar period very shortly, possibly within the next year, and we are going to find our mining industry on a salvage basis. Remember this, that while during the war we have had great metal production in base metals, in such strategic metals as tungsten we shall be unable after the war to compete with the rest of the world, because we have only produced them under the stress of war, because a bigger supply was not available; it was cut off by war. We needed the metals and we needed them at any price; we had to have them. But when the war is over, world sources of these strategic metals will be opened up; it will be found that it will be uneconomic to continue producing a number of them, and in all probability the operations will close down. Some of them have already closed down. The mercury situation is a peculiarly dangerous one; if I may use the word about mercury, it is a peculiarly volatile one, because it fluctuates tremendously, depending upon the outlook and upon certain peculiarities of the industry. Tungsten is another such instance. We have the Emerald mine: having opened up that mine we find that there is no market for its products. There was a market: we had to have the tungsten at that particular time: but at the present time the mine, I believe-the hon. member for Kootenay West will correct me if I am wrong-is closed. That is the sort of thing we are going to find.
The limitation of the credit to base and strategic metals is defeating the very end for which this resolution is required. In the future we shall be worried not so much about getting production of strategic metals as about putting the mining industry back in a sound and a replenishing condition. At the present time, as I have said, the-mining industry in many instances is on a salvage basis.
