The committee resumed at three o'clock.

When the committee rose I had not quite finished what I had to say with regard to this item. One of our most immediate problems, as I have tried to point out to the parliamentary assistant this morning, is not the finding of strategic metals. The operations specially undertaken for war purposes have to a very great degree been closed down because they cannot now compete with the natural source of supply. I mentioned tungsten, molybdenum, mecury, mica and others. These operations are not going to be of much use to us because even now, while the war is on, they cannot continue; so that with the resolution as it now stands the minister is flogging a dead horse. To make the resolution really mean something I would suggest bringing it into line with legislation elsewhere, that expenditures on prospecting be allowed at the rate of 100 per cent. By this I mean that if an individual or a company grubstaked the prospector the whole amount so expended in grubstaking would' be allowed as a deduction. There would have to be some safeguard with regard to the way in which that money was expended. That I see. But in Canada to-day we have active and extremely capable prospectors associations who are jealous of their good name. Not only that, but we have an equally active Canadian institute of mining and metallurgy, and there are the various provincial mining associations. They are all responsible bodies of men and they have a great responsibility to the state. They would join with the government in judging of the bona fides of the prospector. That is the way it has been done elsewhere. I believe that the private association is the one that is recognized in England where legislation similar to that which I have suggested is in force.
Let us see what this means. Mining is a game that is completely unlike any other operation. Mining is one of the few operations, in fact it is the only one I know of, where the small man, the individual who has as little as $50, has an opportunity -to enter into the development of Canada. May I give the minister some figures on the national character of this industry, and I do so to prove the point I wish to make. To-day there are in mining companies 136,801,310 shares. Of that number there are owned in Canada 99,579,476, or 73 per cent; in the United States, 28 million, or 20-5 per cent; elsewhere, 9 million, or 6-5 per cent. This shows that the shares are very largely held in Canada. But it has escaped so many people that there are 274,192 individual shareholders
Income War Tax

in Canadian mines, of which number 168,404 are resident in Canada, while 81,869 are in the United States and about 24,000 elsewhere. In other words, 61-4 per cent of the total number of shareholders reside in Canada. This means that 168,404 individuals are dependent on or have a stake in the mining industry.
There is no other industry anywhere in the world that can show a comparable general and widespread public interest as the mining industry in Canada. It is truly a national industry. The average shareholding of all these people is around 500 shares. These are the facts. It is nationally owned; it is owned by the small man; and it is the one industry that can serve us immediately at the end of the war. Under this clause, however, no encouragement whatsoever is given to the general prospector. You are told you can go and look for molybdenum or tungsten or other strategic minerals knowing that mine after mine is being closed down because they are not economic. Nobody would go into a tungsten mine to-day or into a molybdenum mine. Properties are being closed because the other natural and great source of these metals is being opened up.
If the minister would accept my suggestion and remove the qualifying conditions in this section and allow prospecting for all metals, not merely restricting it to base and strategic metals, it would mean that the prospector could go and benefit by whatever he might find. I wish to urge that very strongly upon the minister. I believe the Minister of Mines and Resources should have been here and should have stressed it as hard as I am, in fact harder, because he can say to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue things which it would be perhaps unparliamentary for me to say. However, I say to the assistant that there is no outlet, there is no field of endeavour that offers the possibility of the mining industry, and it offers it right away.
You will say that there has been a great boom in the Yellowknife and elsewhere. True, there has been a speculative boom, but the Yellowknife has been known for a number of years. The market has certainly reflected a speculative interest in a number of drill holes, but remember, a drill hole is not a mine. Because we are led away by looking at the mining market that is not a sound basis on which to regard the future of this industry. We have to see to it that -the mines are developed. Mere speculation as the result of a drill hole is not development. I leave that with the minister, with the most earnest request that he give it serious consideration before these resolutions are finally passed.
[Mr. Adamson.!

In the few remarks which the Minister of National Revenue made on these resolutions he made it quite clear that he did not make the balls of taxation; he only rolled them. I think in that terse statement I represent clearly the gist of his remarks before the committee. I and others have suggested here to-day that the reason why the line of demarcation, or shall I say discrimination, has been drawn so closely is that it is an administrative one and an administrative one only. It lies within the minister's power to indicate whether that is the real reason why the resolution does not go as far as hon. members have urged. I ask the minister to lay the cards on the table and to say that this is the real reason. Then I suggest to him that a complete answer has not been given to the hon. member for Yukon and others who have indicated a way, in their localities at least, whereby this discrimination may be overcome. A case has been made out for the prospector and his individual backer that is unanswerable. There should be encouragement given to them, because, as the hon. member for York West has just indicated, there is no occupation in the country that can be put into action so quickly and easily immediately after the war as the mining business. Surely we ought to try to encourage that I request the Minister of National Revenue to state the positon frankly. Is not this an ad^ ministrative difficulty?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: No; I would1 not say that at all.
Then what is the real difficulty?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The. parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has answered that question on two occasions.

With due respect to the minister, I do not think he answered it at all. He just said it was a matter of policy on the part of the government, without giving any of the reasons lying behind that policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have tried to do it
several times. I do not think there is any purpose in repeating what I said this morning. Would my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question? Does he think there are not sufficient funds coming forward now for prospecting purposes?-because that of course is all this section covers. It does not affect the individual prospector, as I tried to make clear this morning. It does, I presume, encourage some people to put money into prospecting. Does he from his own experience feel that

Income War Tax
there is not enough money being put up for prospecting purposes? My own opinion is that there is.

My experience would not be worth anything, because I do not come from a mining country and am not interested in mining stock. But those who ought to know and do know say that prospecting is dead. I think it was the parliamentary assistant who said that there were no men available for prospecting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My information is just the contrary. Every prospector in the country is working his head off.

Somebody said there were no prospectors available. I do not believe that for a moment. I believe there will always be an opportunity for prospectors, and as the hon. member for Vancouver South said, after the war there will be many, within a year perhaps, who will want to engage in prospecting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the time to give the incentive.
No; now is the time to give the incentive so that they will know what the position is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My hon. friend realizes that originally this was for one year only, for the 1943 period. This resolution proposes that it be extended for one more year. It is not a permanent part of our taxation legislation and the taxation that has arisen in this war. I should like to quote what the minister said with regard to mining company taxation in his budget speech. I think it is well worth repeating. At page 4182 of Hanard the minister said:
During recent months we have been urged to introduce a number of drastic changes in the tax structure as it affects the mining and oil producing industries. These industries are very properly considering their post-war position and the contribution which they can make to the solution of post-war problems. Needless to say, the government has very much in mind the need of a comprehensive and many-sided programme to encourage the efficient development of our natural resources and to assure that these industries vi 11 make the maximum contribution to the expansion of employment, national income and national wealth after the war. Natural resources, of course, are for the most part in the hands of the provinces, but the dominion, it is believed, can do much to promote full development and wise conservation. Tax policy may be one of the devices which it may appropriately use ti these ends but it will be by no means the only one. The dominion's programme should be part of an integrated programme worked out in cooperation with the provinces. At the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference, this programme, it is proposed, should be discussed with provincial governments and agreement reached as to the contribution to be made by the respective levels of government.
For these reasons I believe that any radical changes in tax policy of special application only to the mining and oil companies would be premature at this time. The Excess Profits Tax Act already includes a special formula for the taxation of oil wells and gold mines. New companies in the metalliferous mining field enjoy a three-year exemption from excess profits tax. In last year's budget we made a number of important concessions to encourage exploration and drilling for oil and also made it possible for mining companies to write off exploration and prospecting expenses incurred in prospecting anywhere in Canada for base-metals or strategic minerals.
That is the provision we are referring to now. I continue:
With this measure of encouragement the oil and mineral industries have been able to make a very important contribution to the country's war effort. They have also been willing to bear their full share of the burden of financing the war and they well recognize, I believe, that the need for war revenue continues at least as great and as urgent as ever. The changes I have announced in respect of income and excess profits taxation and the indications I have given in regard to future tax policy will apply to these -industries as well as to other industrial enterprises and I hope that it may foe possible to announce at the next session of parliament the comprehensive and integrated programme for the development and conservation of natural resources to which I have already referred.
This statement relates to the broad picture of taxation with respect to mining and other companies engaged in developing the natural resources. This particular provision is a limited incentive provision which was inserted in last year's budget provisions for one year only and which rightly or wrongly was felt should be extended for another year. I think my hon. friend from York West will agree-in fact he has already indicated-that this cannot be taken as a broad measure to cover encouragement in general to the mining industry. It was put in because last year it was desired particularly to encourage the prospecting for base metals and so-called strategic metals. That is all the section is. It is not a broad measure to cover the mining industry as a whole. I think it is desirable to renew it for another year. I think it should be considered along with other provisions when there is a discussion with the provinces as to the proper basis for mining companies as a whole.
That means just stalling on the whole proposition. All that has been asked for here to-day is that the discrimination against the private prospector and his backer be removed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There is no discrimination against the private prospector. There may
Income War Tax

be-I am not prepared to admit there is-some discrimination against the backer of the private prospector.
I said -'and his backer".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My answer to that is, whether my hon. friend agrees with it or not, I think in such circumstances the incentive to .abuse would be so great I do not believe it should be introduced.
That means administration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Administration is a necessary part of any tax law, and if a law cannot-
But it is not a fundamental part.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If a tax law cannot be
administered efficiently and fairly, so that the people will believe in it, in my opinion it is a bad tax law.

I just want to refer to
one point. The statement was made that there were enough prospectors. Referring to the official blue book containing the report on reconstruction, I find the significant statement that successful prospecting had almost come to an end after 1940. That is what has happened; successful prospecting has come to an end. I have tried to point out that the great boom in the Yellowknife was the result of a series of diamond drill holes, which may or may not mean a mine there. Until we have the definite development we cannot tell. I repeat that prospecting has virtually ceased in a great part of Canada, other than some special sections where I admit there is a good deal of activity at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Certainly I cannot say with any personal knowledge whether or not prospecting has ceased. My officials tell me that according to their information that is not the case. Of course it may have been curtailed because of the man-power shortage, but I cannot say as to that.

Will the assistant to the
minister inform me whether I am correct in assuming that the write-off is designed to encourage prospecting in regard to base metals, and not in regard to gold?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.

Then I should like to make this contribution, if it be one, to the discussion. My experience is that prospecting has practically dried up. It is my view that prospecting for gold mines should be encouraged now, instead of waiting until the war is over. It has

been said previously, and I do not want to go all over it again, that from the time the prospector is lucky enough or scientific enough to stake out a claim, at least four years must elapse before the mine can be brought into production. I took the trouble to elaborate on this point on another occasion; I am not going over it again, but I do not think anyone who understands mining will dispute that statement.
Four years is a very short time.

It is probably the minimum length of time, according to all our experience with silver in the old Cobalt days, with gold in the various gold camps, and with base metals. If it be right to encourage prospecting for gold, why should we wait until the war is over, and then have a further hiatus of four years before any more gold properties can be brought into production? After the war our friends to the south may not be as liberal with us as they have been up to the present in the matter of credit. They have given us splendid cooperation so far; we have been enabled to make goods for the mother country because the United States have given us credit for the raw materials we required. However, notwithstanding what may happen at Bretton Woods, in the natural course of events that cooperation will begin to taper off to some extent. Then we may be told again by the Minister of Finance, as the predecessor of the present minister, who is now Minister of National Defence, told the gold mining industry two or three years ago, "Spend your money. Increase your plants. Take on all the men you can. Produce every ounce of gold you can possibly produce to enable us to maintain our exchange with the United States at something like a reasonable level, because we have to do it." What is going to be the use of that if we are to be blacked out for a four year interval after the war? I do suggest to the Minister of Finance and his associates that this matter should be given some further consideration.
Now I should like to say a word about the suggestion that there are no prospectors available to go into the field, if they could do so under attractive conditions. It is true that there is a sprinkling of prospectors in the armed forces. Those in the north country who were of army age flocked to the colours; there was no more loyal body of men in the country. But there is a vast army of prospectors who are over military age, but who, because of their experience, are still extremely useful. Indeed, without throwing any stones at the younger men, I might say the older ones are

Income War Tax
perhaps even more useful. If you take the trouble to go back through the statistics and look up the prospectors who have been most prominent in discovering valuable mineral properties of all types throughout Canada for the last thirty years, you will find that in the main the original discoveries were made by men of fifty years of age and over. In other words the old timer, of whom we speak in the mining camps, is still with us. If you would give him proper encouragement he would go all over the country carrying on his work. I want to join with those who have said that we have not understood the encouragement we ought to give those prospectors. I fail to appreciate why we should continue to encourage men to look for base metals, which we will require to a much smaller extent after the war, and at the same time refuse to encourage men to prospect for gold, which we will require to a far greater extent after the war.

In rising to support the suggestions that have been made by various hon. members I should like to say that I hope the spirit behind this section will be embodied in our post-war taxation legislation. This house has been reminded already, but I will take time to repeat it, that eighty-four per cent of our mineral production is coming from mines discovered before 1920. As the hon. member for Parry Sound just said, prospecting is at a standstill, and nothing we could do would be better calculated to open up our great north country than to have more prospectors. However, I should like to direct my remarks to the suggestion that there should not be any substantial administrative difficulty in extending the benefits of this provision to the individual prospector who is backed by another individual or a small group of people. The parliamentary assistant has suggested that such a provision would be full of loopholes, that a father might send his son into the woods on a vacation, to fish, and he would be able to get an allowance in his taxation bracket under the pretext of having sent his boy out on a prospecting expedition. I do not believe such things are likely to occur. Of course there may be a few cases of that kind, but I do not believe their number would be at all substantial. I think the parliamentary assistant or the Minister of National Revenue, who is in charge of the enforcement of this provision, should outline some of the cases which they fear will deprive the treasury of a substantial amount of revenue.
Let us analyse the case of the father and son. Is a father going to give his boy S500, or some such amount, to go into the north country and spend his summer fishing, and then
claim this $500 as a deduction from his income tax? In the first place that would mean that a father would have to be in collusion with his son in an effort to cheat the government out of a certain amount of money. I doubt very much if there are many fathers in this country who would be willing to conspire with their sons for such a purpose. I think the fears of the Department of Revenue are ill-founded. I heard just the other day of an interesting story about a saw mill owner who was said to have forty bosses and who operated at a loss. I could not understand how that could be, but it was explained to me that he was in the habit of taking logs out of the river which did not belong to him. His employees knew about that, and they proceeded according to their own ideas as to how long or how hard they should work. The result was that he was certainly worse off than if he had operated as an honest man.
I doubt very much if dishonesty would further any person in this game of sending a man into the north country, any more than it would in any other field. In my view the fears of the department are entirely without foundation, and I would ask for information as to other eases than that of the father and son, which has been mentioned. What man is going to give some other person $400 or $500 to go up to the north country to waste? People are not disposed that way. I should think any attempt at collusion would be pretty well confined to a family, and I have endeavoured to explain that the honour existing between father and son would be such as to prevent any great number of these cases at any rate. Furthermore, if the Department of National Revenue would undertake a few prosecutions, where there may be loopholes, they would soon find that there would be no more advantage taken of those so-called loopholes, and the result would be a stimulus to exploration and prospecting activity in this country, something which is so badly needed for the post-war period.
The department has admitted the principle that we need more prospecting in the north country7. An extension is granted to companies and syndicates which are registered, but refused to individuals. I call upon the department to review its decision to exclude advances to individuals to encourage prospecting, as having been based upon ill-founded fears. The administration must not consider itself first, even if there are some who do slip through their meshes. The important thing is the matter of job creation, and the bringing of more production to the market, whether it be of minerals or any other commodity, which will help the standard of living of the people.
Income War Tax

That is the important thing. We must recognize that man is not made for the budget, but rather the budget is made for man. And where there may be more production, it must not be restricted by considerations based upon ill-founded fears in the minds of officers in the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue.
Mr. BLACK (Yukon)! The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has made it quite clear that the government will continue its policy of discriminating against contributions by taxpayers to individual prospectors. I do not think there is any mistake about that. To my mind that is a poor policy, and one which will not tend to increase mineral production in this country. I said in the first place that it was unfair, and I say it should not be continued. This morning I suggested to the government a veiy simple way in which they can remove the difficulty so far as the administration is concerned. It was my understanding that the Minister of National Revenue said that this provision of the Income War Tax Act, subsection 5 of section 8, will be extended to apply to the Yukon territory and the Northwest territories, as it does now to the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is correct, yes.

I can see the difficulty in the minds of the Minister of National Revenue and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance in understanding the pleas which have been placed before them to-day. From what they have said, they envisage the big man in Montreal or Toronto or Hamilton who puts up 8100,000 or $50,000, or some other large sum of money-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is limited to $5,000.

*-to help out a prospector. But the situation we are asking the government to meet is entirely different. We are thinking of the small town of perhaps 500 or 1,000 people, where there are young men, or perhaps older men, who know the country, understand prospecting and are willing to go out and take a chance in the hope of finding a bonanza. That is the way the mines in British Columbia were found. As a matter of fact, in many instances these individual prospectors are in direct competition with the prospectors sent out by the big companies. Mind you, that is heavy competition, because the big companies in the event of a strike in a district may send out twenty-five or fifty employees to stake everything in sight. In some cases they keep the little fellow right out of the field.

We are asking for help for the individual prospector who will go out from the small towns. In the first place, we think his backer, the local merchant who puts up the food or an amount of cash, should be entitled to this tax credit. I go further and say that the man himself who goes out should be entitled to his expenses as a credit. This morning the parliamentary assistant said that he thought that was already done. I am informed that it is not. The prospector spends his money in the purchase of food and mining equipment, but does not get any credit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The deputy minister tells me that under those circumstances a man is entitled to the expenses entailed in earning his income.
But is he entitled to his food? Is he entitled to the amount he pays for food?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He is entitled to ordinary equipment, whatever expense he incurs, just the same as you and I as lawyers are entitled to our expenses in earning legal fees.

But we are not entitled to the cost of our food. This man would be going out and taking a chance. For instance, let us consider the man returning from the war who has a small amount of money coming in from other sources, which will be taxed very heavily. There is no chance that he will use that money to go out and risk it in the hills. I suggest he should be given a tax credit just to aid him in prospecting. Those are the cases we are worried about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Upon what does the hon. member say he should get a tax credit?
For his expenses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He gets that now. From what would it come?
Well, if we can be sure he gets it, that helps.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He does get it.
But I do not think he does.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This section gives tax assistance to the man who puts up the money to help some person to do the prospecting.
I am referring to the prospector himself; does he get an allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean a credit from the income he earns from his prospecting?

In making out his income tax return each year, does he get credit for what he had to spend in order to equip himself to go out prospecting?

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: If he has earned income from his going out and prospecting, he does. That is what he can deduct expenses from, namely, the expense incurred in earning that income.
In many cases the prospector goes out but does not earn an income.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Then he is not taxable. What could he put the tax credit against then?
Any other income he has.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: No; he cannot do that.

Then he is not getting any help at all under the present law. That is the picture. I cannot understand why you help the big companies but will not help the little fellow. So far as we are concerned that is all wrong and certainly should be remedied.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I just make one point clear? My hon. friend has referred to the big companies, but if he will look at the resolution he will see that they are not necessarily big companies. A big company may get the benefit of it, but it says:
That the tax credit allowed to a taxpayer of forty per centum of contributions made by him in the year 1943 to associations, syndicates or mining partnerships registered or otherwise recognized under the law of any province in Canada.
That is pretty broad. Take the case of a small town, such as my hon. friend mentioned, and of a group who want to grubstake a prospector. It is perfectly open to them to register as a mining partnership in accordance with the law of the province. They can put their capital into this partnership, and the partnership may engage a prospector and grubstake him to go out. Contributions or payments to a mining partnership, a prospecting syndicate or whatever you want to call it, would qualify under this section. The limitations under the section are twofold. First, there is a restriction as to base or strategic metals, and we had some discussion on that point. Second, the credit is not allowed in the case of contributions made to individuals. It has been urged strongly by the hon. member for Yukon and others that this credit should be extended to contributions or subscriptions to individuals. I have endeavoured to put forward, perhaps unsatisfactorily, the reason why it was decided last year after consideration that that should not be done, and that the same considerations ruled this year. But that is the only limitation. As I have pointed out, it covers associations, syndicates or mining partnerships registered or otherwise recognized under the laws of any province of Canada.
Mr. GREE'N: The parliamentary assistant stated this morning that he is opposed to this tax credit because in the large cities promoters are using it for their own purposes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Please do not misquote me. I did not say they were using it. I expressed my personal opinion, which I have always had, that it gave a certain amount of incentive to stock promoters to form these syndicates or associations for the purpose of getting subscriptions from the public on the ground that they would be partly exempt from taxation. That is only my own personal opinion. I think that objection is more than overcome by the desirability of encouraging this work.
That objection would not be applicable in the case of a merchant in a town who advanced money to a prospector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There are other objections that are equally strong.
In that case it is not a question of financing or floating a company.

I am going to move an amendment to this resolution which I think will resolve some of the difficulties we are up against. I move:
That the word "base" be struck out of clause 30.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not an expert on parliamentary procedure, but I think this is a money resolution, and if it is-
It is a tax resolution; it is not expending money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am in the hands of the committee.
That is a new doctrine, that a private member cannot amend a tax resolution. I have seen it done fifty times.
Not if it increases-

The hon. member is no authority on anything as far as I am concerned. If he will just keep quiet I will explain my position. If this resolution provided for the expenditure of public money, then the parliamentary assistant's point might be well taken.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is attempting to amend a tax exemption.
A resolution providing ways and means of raising money is in an entirely different category.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This is a resolution which provides a tax credit.
Income War Tax
This resolution is the reverse of one to raise money; this resolution gives some relief.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It affects the revenue.

I do not agree with that. If that is to be the case we might just as well fold up and go home as far as these tax resolutions are concerned. It will be ridiculous if parliament is to be hamstrung in that respect. The rule is that no one but' a member of the government can introduce such a resolution, but that does not say that we cannot amend it. I have seen time after time motions put in committee of the whole to reduce an item in the estimates to one dollar.
That is in order.
Thank you for the commendation; I am glad to hear that you agree with me. This amendment is of the same nature.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I rise to a point of order?
I am not through yet.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I was going to help you.

I hope you are, but wait until I am through. I am a little fearful of help from that quarter, but I will welcome it if it is genuine. The illustration I gave about reducing the estimate is I submit on a parallel with this amendment. I hope the parliamentary assistant will not be serious in pressing his point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
An amendment to reduce an estimate simply provides that we spend less money, and it is open to any hon. member to move such an amendment. But this resolution affects the revenue. If the exemption is extended to other classes than have been provided, then the revenue will be affected. I prefaced what I said with the remark that I am no expert on parliamentary procedure but I have always understood that a money resolution or a resolution affecting the revenue had to be introduced by a member of the government and had to be preceded by the formula we have listened to on many occasions, that it has been communicated to His Excellency the Governor General, and so on. This is a resolution which affects the revenue. The suggestion made by the hon. member for York West would have the effect of diminishing the revenue which would be

received under the Income War Tax Act. If that is so, then I think it would be out of order.

I suggest that we
should know just what the amendment is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved by the

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Whether or not a point
of order has been raised, I should like to refer to citation 502 in the third edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. I am not discussing the merits of the amendment moved by the hon. member for York West, but I should like to read this citation:

On the

Perhaps they will be less stubborn about making changes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not know whether
the hon. member for York West had concluded what he had to say, and perhaps I should not have interrupted him. After he has completed his remarks I would prefer that the committee allow the resolution to stand until the minister is able to be here.

I want to make two short statements. The Australia act describes exactly what a prospector is. It is not easy to be a prospector. There are prospectors' associations in the various provinces which are very jealous of their good name. If the government are going to cooperate and allow a credit for money spent in prospecting, then I think they will find the prospectors' associations and the mining associations extremely jealous. They will be careful to see that their good names are maintained and that no money earmarked for prospecting is spent in any other way. To that extent I am certain of the genuineness of the prospectors' associations.
Now I come to the amendment. A prospector goes out into the field. In our complex geological structure he may be looking for anything-copper, zinc, molybdenum, tungsten or half a dozen other base metals, and he may find a showing of precious metals mixed with base metals. Nickel is a case in point, also

Income War Tax
Noranda and Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting. All have a definite precious metal content in their ores. Frequently base metal mines have started out because it was thought they were precious metal mines. If you continue to have this limiting clause, when a prospector finds a showing of precious metals when he is out looking for base metals, he will turn it down because he can get no allowance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The individual prospector gets no concession under this. It is his backer that gets it.
In nearly every case you will find that the prospector is in part his own backer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If he found a showing of precious metals I doubt that he would quit simply because he could not get the benefit of this exemption.

It depends on the showing. You can never tell what you are going to find. In some gold areas some of our biggest base metal mines have been discovered, and vice versa. That is why I say that this amendment should be given very serious consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The section might stand
until the minister can be here. But I just want to say one word about the individual prospector. Mrs. MacMillan is the president of the Dominion Prospectors' Association, and her association has never requested that this be extended to the individual prospector. I am advised that one reason why they have not done so is that they feel it might bring the section into disrepute and result in the concession being withdrawn entirely. I just wanted to get that on the record.
They are fearful of abuse.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: These prospectors' associations, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury knows, are extremely well organized in each province, and we have had no request from a single prospectors' association that this concession should be extended to the individual prospector.	,

You have this
request from the members of this house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, but we have had no request from any of the associations referred to.
These associations might not be interested in private individuals, merchants and others, who desire to grubstake the .prospectors.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would think that most of the prospectors would be members of the associations and therefore that the associations of prospectors would be interested in the backers of individual prospectors to have this concession extended which is given to syndicates and partnerships. I just wanted to point out that we have had no such representations from any of these associations.
I am surprised, because that certainly is not the story that was intimated to me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

That is the information

speechtext:
In any case I have asked that the resolution stand, so that the minister himself might consider the amendment.
Resolution stands.
31. That one-half of expenditures on maintenance and repairs incurred by any taxpayer carrying on a business (or an underground development, in the case of a taxpayer operating a mine) in a period to be fixed by order in council be regarded as deferred maintenance and repairs and be deductible as an expense, at the option of the taxpayer, either in the year or fiscal periods when incurred or in years or fiscal periods ending subsequent to December 31, 1942.

This is a very important matter which was referred to by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. His remarks will be found at the beginning of the last paragraph on page 4181 of Hansard. Just to refresh the minds of hon. gentlemen I am going to read what the minister said, and make, I hope, a few appropriate comments. He said:
Another point at which our taxes on business income have gone beyond the taxation of true income, is an the matter of expense for maintenance and repairs.
That is a sad admission, that the taxation policy of the country has in that regard gone
Income War Tax

beyond the taxation of true income; that is, it is violating the real principles of taxation. The minister went on:
For the past two years, in certain industries at least, it has been impossible, by reason of shortages of material and labour and the necessity of continuous operations-
That is in industry itself.
-to carry out the maintenance and repair work that would be normal and necessary to prevent the deterioration of plant and equipment.
That is quite true; there is no doubt about it, and I would say that it goes beyond the past two years. The minister went on :
As a result, deferred maintenance expense is accumulating, and, in the meantime, profits are inflated because full maintenance is not charged.
That I think is a true statement of the position. Apparently the minister's advisers are properly informed of what the position is. The only remark I would make about that is that it is an understatement of the position. Full maintenance is not charged, deferred maintenance expense is very rapidly accumulating, and profits are thereby tremendously inflated and are taxed improperly, taxed in some cases 100 per cent less the 20 per cent refundable. That is a serious indictment against the present taxation structure. The minister goes on to say:
We have 'tried in the past to find some equitable formula for permitting the setting up of a maintenance reserve, but it is extremely difficult to devise one which will fit the varying circumstances of all industry.
I suppose that is an administrative difficulty, but I see no difficulty in devising a formula that would operate for a particular industry, and I do not understand why it has not been permitted before. The minister goes on:
We are now recommending a provision for the future which 1 hope will meet the -problem in at least a partial way-
I suggest that that is not good enough. I characterized it in my address on the budget as a pseudo remedy, and I adhere to that term for lack of a better one. Here you have an admission by the minister of a weakness in the tax structure and that he is attempting to meet the problem merely in a partial way which will speed up the work of plant repair in a period when additional employment may be needed. What is the proposal?
The proposal is that one-half the expenditure on maintenance and repairs, incurred in a period to be fixed by the governor in council-
I pause here to criticize the giving of authority to have the period fixed by the governor in council. How can the governor in council-which means the Department of National Revenue, which means the commis-
sioner and his staff-know iwhat is to be the appropriate period? Yet they make the final and only decision. The man who should be able to fix it definitely in his own particular case is the man who wants to catch up on the deferred maintenance, not a government bureau. What is the parliamentary assistant's answer to that indictment of bureaucratic power, a power which is reserved in this resolution, purposely and with intent aforethought, according to the minister's statement as it appears at page 4181. They are to hold the strings in their hands, and if their opinion differs from' that of the proprietors of the business, then the latter are overruled and the department is the sole judge. I continue the quotation:
-may be charged against the income of a previous fiscal period but not farther back than the fiscal periods ending in 1943. In the case of the mining industry, maintenance and repairs will be held to include also underground development work.
I am not concerned about that at the moment. Now I submit that we are entitled to a much fuller explanation than is contained either in the minister's statement or in the resolution before us. The resolution before us takes an arbitrary half of the expenditures on deferred maintenance and repairs and carries into effect this period to be fixed by order in council and to be deductible as expense at the taxpayer's option in any fiscal year within the limitations mentioned.' We should have a thorough explanation of this half remedy, according to the minister's own admission. I call it a pseudo remedy, because it is not a real remedy at all but a partial remedy. Perhaps his language is better than mine. It is a partial remedy for what he admits, in his statement at page 4181, to be an evil in the tax structure. He admits that the tax structure on business income has gone beyond the true measure of taxation on true income. That is a damning admission, in the minister's own words, that they have overtaxed companies in previous years. They have not allowed sufficient sums to take care of what is a necessary provision for maintenance and repairs, which must foe deferred because of the lack of labour or perhaps equipment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is why it is being corrected now.
Yes, but it is only to the extent of one half of what it ought to be.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Oh, no.

Oh, yes. The parliamentary assistant can explain it if he likes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You can have it one half in one year and one half in another.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

I am
strong on denunciation, because it is the only way to get at the truth-that and crossexamination. You cannot get it by mealy-mouthed phrases or polite invitations. You never get anywhere. It is justifiable.

In many cases it is justifiable. I will not waste more time on that because I think I have made my point.
To come to section 31 of the resolution, I do not wish to go over the whole ground again, but we have first of all a frank admission on the part of the Minister of Finance that they have been doing an injustice through the tax structure to corporations and companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Only if perpetuated. Be fair.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Only if it is not corrected.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall have a word to say on that.

I read the English language and I try to understand it and I think I have some realization of the value of words. He says:
Our taxes on business income have gone beyond the taxation of true income.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: But that is because they have not been able to get materials to do repairs, and we are recognizing that fact.

This indictment in the Winnipeg Free Press was published in March of this year. It contains at least three of the most damning indictments that I have ever heard put forward to the public of this country, and it is published by one of the

strongest supporters of this government. They may have some underlying reason for this indictment; I do not know. I am not in the confidence of the Siftons, but on the surface it speaks for itself.
Let me call this to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. The first count in the indictment is that our -tax laws are undemocratic. That is a very general statement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is that on this resolution?
I think I can talk about taxation on this resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We must have reached the stage now after so many months of the session where we should keep within the ambit of the resolution that is before the committee.

You are doing yourself credit.

If you have anything to say about me, get up in your place and say it and I will answer it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That could be done under any section of the resolution?
I think it could. I think you can attack the system of taxation under any section.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Again with deference I would differ, but perhaps I am wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It can be said on the second reading of the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt
my hon. friend, but if we can have the general criticism on the second reading of the bill perhaps it would facilitate the resolutions.

Before the Chairman rules I shall answer that by referring my hon. friend to what the Minister of Finance said about this very proposal at page 4181 of Hansard when he delivered his budget speech. He was referring to the point I have raised. This is what he said:
. . . our taxes on business income have gone beyond the taxation of true income. . . .
Using that basis laid down by the Minister of Finance, under which this resolution is brought in, I propose to indict the taxation system, if I am permitted.
