speechtext:
On the point of order,
in the committee of ways and means it is easy for hon. members to have a general discussion on almost any resolution but it is not conducive to celerity. The hon. member for York-Sunbury knows the rules better than I do myself-

I -would
not say that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
He realizes that I am
the last man who would try to curtail discussion. I am in the hands of the committee. I know they want to play fair in their deliberations. It is absolutely impossible to have ironbound rules. However,' I believe at this stage of the deliberations it should be possible to keep within the ambit of the resolution before the committee and avoid general discussion not germane to the clause.

Then I
take it if I keep within the ambit of the subject matter of the resolution I am in order in proceeding, and I shall be glad to do so.
I lay down the first indictment against the proposal as outlined by the government's

Income War Tax
friend, the Winnipeg Free Press, that our tax laws are undemocratic. This is what the Free Press says:
In the Minister of National Revenue-which actually means in his deputy and other officials-
I hope the minister is not just a figurehead, but that is the implication here.
-the law vests almost dictatorial powers.
That, of course, is the gravamen of the charge, and I think there is a large measure of truth in it.
-almost dictatorial powers; and not only dictatorial powers but sweeping powers of discretion.
I say it is an axiom of any taxation statute that the right to tax must be clear and explicit as against the subject; unless it is, the courts of this country will not give effect to the power to tax. That is one of the fundamental principles of the right of the crown to tax the subject. That has been departed from so frequently and to such a degree in the growing powers of income taxation that we have in this country that it calls not only for an immediate halt but for reform, which is long overdue. I have not the section of the act before me, but in a given case certain government bureaux of this country are entitled to impose taxation that is not imposed by the statute itself; not only that, but to fix the rate and the incidence of taxation. That is taxation outside of the borders of the statute itself. That was done, it was said, to meet a special case of tax evasion. I think that was the reason for it, and there is some basis for that reason, but why give it to a group of men, no matter how much confidence we may have in their personal character? It is wrong in principle to give power such as that to a group of men when parliament has not even been consulted about it. This article goes on to say:
In a democratic country the citizen should never be subjected, if law can prevent it, to the varying opinions of officials, however sincere-
That is exactly what I have been saying in other language. That is the position to-day. In this country citizens are subjected to the varying opinions of officials and perhaps to the varying opinions of the same officials; although I am bound to say I have not before me an instance that would justify me in being dogmatic about that statement, because I have found that once a decision is given it is like the law of the Medes and Persians; they very rarely reverse themselves. They think it is not proper to do so. Well, let me say to the minister that in one of the greatest courts the world has ever seen, the Supreme Court of the United States, they do
reverse themselves. We are not so good at that sort of thing in Canada, we are so bound by precedent; but in reading the history of the Supreme Court of the United States and its place in the history of that country I have been struck by the number of times that that court has reversed itself. I do not think that ever happens in the income tax department of this country.
Then the article refers to the matter which I brought up in this house last week, namely, the inadequate system of appeals against the arbitrary decisions of tax officials. That is the language of the Free Press, not mine. I did not go as far as that, nor am I going as far as that now. It was the system of appeals that I was objecting to, which the parliamentary assistant characterized, I think, as an empty gesture, or something to that effect; at least, that it was not worth while.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said the worst that could be said about it was that it was a bit of waste motion.

I cannot remember the words my hon. friend used, but I know he gave half-hearted assent to my proposal. The Minister of National Revenue proposed to perpetuate that system making him the sole court of appeal, if I understood him correctly last week, but having a group of technical advisers around him, which of course does not meet the point at all. The next point made by the Free Press is:
Again, twenty-six years after assessing a citizen for taxes, the government can reopen the account and, saying it was mistaken in the first place, force him to pay more taxes for years long past.
That has not been amended, except with respect to men overseas, and for that much consideration we give thanks.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That has been amended.

There
should be some limitation. I point out that this is not permitted in Great Britain or the United States. I think that is based on the theory that the principle of estoppal does not operate against the crown. I never could understand why that should be so, why the principle of estoppal should not operate against the crown as it does against me as a subject. It is a survival of the old days when the crown was supreme, when it could do anything it liked and was not amenable to the ordinary laws of the country. The doctrine that the principle of estoppal should not apply against the crown should be thrown into the discard immediately, for it is a denial of justice.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member has not read resolution No. 20.

I have read it but perhaps I have not comprehended it fully. You know, they were passed through within three minutes after the house met the other evening, before many hon. members got to the chamber.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: But we went back to a number of them.
To No. 15.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And two or three others.

I have looked at resolution 20, and I am corrected to a degree; but if I am permitted to say what I would have said if I had been here when that resolution was called, I suggest that the six year limitation should date from the filing of the assessment, and not from the assessment itself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member for Rose-dale put forward that argument the other night.

He is putting it forward again through me now, and that is the criticism I am going to make. This change has partly taken care of the objections of the Free Press, and I am not going to labour the point further. On the other hand, supposing after I pay my tax I find that I have overpaid; what right have I to ask the government to reopen my assessment? I think they would do it; I have enough faith in the fairness of the administrative officers of the department to believe that if I could show that I had made an overpayment they would reopen the case and give me a refund, but there is no right on the part of the subject. I think that is a correct statement; and as a corollary to the crown's right to reopen, provision should be made for the subject's right to reopen. That would seem to me to be a balanced position.
Then the provision for refunds is discretionary. Well, I think the Free Press is wrong when it says the government "may" make the refund; I would believe the word "may" as it applies to the crown in effect would be mandatory, and that they must make the refund, so that I am not going to add that count to the indictment against the government.
There is this matter of the charging of interest on deficiency payments. I could tell a long story in that connection, but I hope the matter is going before the courts, so that I am not going to deal with it here. But if the government charges interest on deficiency

payments why should it not allow interest on overpayments? That is a point which I think cries for reform, and I do hope the officials will give effect to that change. It seems to me that is only fair and just. It used to be that if you made an overpayment you got a refund, if the assessment was made within a reasonable time. To-day they put the overpayment to your credit for the next taxing year, long before it is due. That reminds me of the story told me by an old Irish woman who was employed to do the washing in my mother's home; she was paid so much per diem-not so much either, in the light of what is paid to-day. She had to use a certain portion of that money for the final repose of her husband's soul, a most exemplary thing for her to do. I was just a lad, and I asked how she knew when the payments were completed. She replied that she never knew, but that if she overpaid it went to the credit of her next friend. That was her opinion; it may be wrong, but that is the story of which I am reminded. In this case the government exercises some option the authority for which I cannot find in any statute, and instead of making a refund of the overpayment it is credited to the tax for the next year, on the theory that during the time that has elapsed you have again become indebted to the crown, although the amount is ascertained.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: They are entitled to their money at once if they want it.
Then why, without asking, do they put it through as a credit for the following year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: They get their assessment; they are shown that it is to their credit, and if they want it back immediately they can have it.
I can show the minister an assessment on which it is indicated that there has been an overpayment, with the statement that it is carried forward to the next taxing year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is quite all right; it is just a matter of convenience. If the taxpayer wants it back he is entitled to it.

I say it is not quite all right at all; the money should come back with the assessment. That is what a business firm would do. If I sent a cheque in payment of an account and overpaid it, my creditor on discovering the error would receipt the bill and return the excess payment. If he did not I would think he was a pretty poor citizen. That is all I am going to say on that point.

Income War Tax
Then, of course, there is the second indictment, which is the strongest of all; that is, the injustice of a system which taxes the same income twice. I suppose it is perfectly useless to argue this point here, but I know it is a great injustice. We passed a convention the other day one of the objects of which was to prevent triple taxation, but as far as I can see no one has raised his voice against the injustice of double taxation. I well remember when that system of double taxation was introduced in this house. I should like to commend to the taxing authorities of this country a review of the position in Great Britain and of the effect of the system here.
I have in my hand a little pamphlet which has been compiled just recently. I am not going to read any part of it; I have not time to do so, but I commend it to the taxation authorities. It is a memorandum on the relationship between an incorporated company and its shareholders, and in regard to the incidence of the United Kingdom income tax and surtax. It- is prepared) by Mr. Raymond W. Needham, one of His Majesty's counsel, and a bencher of the Middle Temple. It has to do with this matter and kindred subjects.
It would be perfectly useless for me to argue the point of double taxation now. But until there is a review of the tax structure in this country, and until some indication is given to the business world as to what the taxation system is to be in the immediate post-war period, nobody can plan for the post-war world so far as industry is concerned. They cannot plan as to what they shall do. I know companies that are just waiting to know what the post-war policy of taxation will be. I made a speech in the house on the budget debate and touched upon that point. I have recalled that the Minister of Finance made the statement that no government could bind its successors. In a general way that is true. But any government, visualizing the post-war period in this country, should indicate at least what its views may be in the post-war period in respect of taxation. I talked that matter over with one of the biggest executives in Canada. If I were to mention his name he would be recognized at once as one of the soundest business men in Canada. I gave him my speech to read, and when he had finished he said, "You are absolutely right. In the businesses of which I am chairman"-and he named three big companies-"we do not know what to do with regard to the post-war period, uptil there is some announcement as to what post-war taxation is to be, and with regard to improving conditions to make employment for people
who are coming back to industry." This is a matter of vital importance to Canada, but nobody is giving any consideration to it, and least of all the government of the day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It has been given constant consideration.

Well, then, they are hiding their light under a bushel. They may be giving theoretical consideration to it. The only thing we are getting is a saturation of taxation-and we certainly have got that. I am going to tell the parliamentary assistant and his colleagues on the treasury benches and members of this government who are now in the chamber that they will know what the public think about it at the next election-make no mistake about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Don't commence to boast.
I am not commencing to boast or to threaten. I am just stating the facts as I hear them from every point, and as I will hear them right in Vancouver Centre.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I will take my chances with you any day.
Come on down and we will fight it out. I will take one side of the ring and you can have the other.
And with one hand tied behind your back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You do not want to pay until it hurts any more.
As far as I am concerned I am paying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And so am I.

I am
paying because I want to help. But I am afraid there are a lot of people in this country to-day who do not want to pay. I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in this house either last session or the session before; I have listened to speeches from other parts of the house, and I have come to the conclusion that there is a certain amount of public opinion in this country that neither wants to pay nor wants to fight to win this war. And that is a pretty sad thing to contemplate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Are you arguing that now?
No, I am condemning it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Taxes are too high, are they?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have given a lot of latitude to this discussion.

Thank
you; I realize that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He is taking it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am in duty bound, however, to consider the rules, and to have hon. members in the committee observe them as closely as possible. Surely the hon. member for York-Sunbury will realize that most of the discussion-although he has made a fine speech, and all that-was not relevant to the subject matter of the resolution.

Thank
you, Mr. Chairman. It will be understood that the last five or ten minutes has been the result of interjections by the Minister of National Revenue. However, I am going to take the chairman's hint, and not wear out my welcome-or perhaps it is not a welcome.
The third point is an indictment against the question of annuities. We shall have something to say about that when the section is under consideration.
There is no section.

Well, we shall have something to say about it at some appropriate time, because I understand the government is setting up a commission to investigate the whole matter. On that point I should like to know just when that is going to happen Why^ is the commission to be set up? I should have thought the department would have had all the facts and could have evolved a formula to submit to parliament. Apparently there is some disagreement. However I am not going on with that.
I am leaving out the fourth point in the indictment in connection with the intolerance and injustice of our tax system as portrayed by the Winnipeg Free Press, a friend of this government. I hope the government will listen to it, and I hope each member of the government has read it.
I shall now return to a brief discussion of the resolution.
Hear, hear.

Well, 1 hope I have not been foolish in what I have said to-day. I hope it has been informative. It is something 1 have thought about for a long time, and something I have thought should be said in the house. I did not hear anyone saying it. It was in the same posi-
[The Chairman.]
tion as the indemnities question. I pointed out last week that what I had said about indemnities was what we were all thinking.
No.

Well,
most of us. I know the hon. member for Sirncoe East does not agree with me. But ninety per cent of the members agreed with what I said about indemnities.
What is the hon. member's authority for the figure of ninety per cent?
I gathered that in a general way, because of the support I got in the house. All parties spoke for it. There was support from all shades of political opinion.
But only about ten spoke.

The others did not have a chance. Some members never speak in the house, but that does not prevent their revealing what is in their minds.
To get down to resolution 31, I should like to have an explanation from the government as to why they limit this to one-half, and why in particular they keep to themselves the power of fixing the period of years. I may have something to say after the reply has been given.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In the first place, as the
minister indicated in his speech, many suggestions have been received from industries which want to be allowed to set up a tax-free reserve to take care of maintenance and repairs they are unable to carry out now because of a shortage of materials and man-power. This matter was carefully considered. The feasibility of being able to allow such a tax-free reserve was considered, and it was felt that the difficulties in the way of allowing it were almost insuperable.
What were they?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
One was that if you allow
a reserve you are permitting the judgment of managements to determine what is adequate provision for repairs and maintenance.
Who would know better?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Whereas under ordinary
circumstances you have the facts as to what money was actually spent on those repairs.
In a given year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The proposal here is that
after a period determined by the governor in

Income War Tax
council repairs and maintenance may be charged, half back to a previous year. In other words the income tax return for that year may be reopened. One-half of the repairs in a given period may be charged back to that year and, in effect, the taxpayer would be receiving a refund on taxes.

Even
though the money is not actually spent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Oh. the money must all be
spent, and the taxpayer may then charge half of it as current and take half of it and put it back in a previous period.	.
When can he do that, in view of the fact that he cannot get either labour or material?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Now I shall meet my hon. friend's second point, the reason for putting in a provision that this will apply during a period to be determined by the governor in council. That period will be fixed when materials and) labour are available and when it is desired to encourage employment. Let us assume for the sake of argument that the war should end some time next year. Materials and labour would then become available for deferred maintenance. The government, would say, "You knew what the provisions were; as and from July 1, 1945, expenditures for deferred maintenance and repairs may be charged in accordance with the provisions of this section; one-half of the expenditure from that date on may at the option of the taxpayer be charged as an expense for any year subsequent to December 31, 1942." The taxpayer is given the option to charge to any year where he had war-time profits but where he was not able to make repairs and do the maintenance which he would ordinarily have been able to do. In other words they are allowing him to put it back into that year, but he has actually to make the repairs or do the maintenance. Then he takes the other half and puts it in the year in which he expends the money.

He is
allowed the full portion of the cost of all maintenance and repairs that he makes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
There is no limitation on that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No. He can take half of it and put it back into a previous period. I have discussed this with a number of concerns that have been unable to make these expenditures for deferred maintenance, and they feel that this will be a real help.
I would not minimize it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not know whether they would have preferred a reserve-, but they seemed to indicate that this will largely meet their problem. I just wanted to clear up my hon. friend's point. The legislation does not contemplate that it shall be chargeable only to the year in which the repairs and maintenance are made; half the expenditure may be taken back into a previous period.

I cannot read into the resolution all that the parliamentary assistant has said but at least his explanation makes it more -understandable. I have discussed this matter with three different lines of industry, and I was told that they would prefer to be allowed to set up reserves. I think that would be the usual method of accounting, would it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The Income War Tax Act has never allowed contingent reserves as a deduction from income. The only reserves that are allowed are those for bad debts and depreciation. The English act is the same.
I do not think that is quite correct -in practice. There is the question of inventory reserves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That has been under the Excess Profits Tax Act since the war began.
They are allowed to set up a reserve for inventories which -have become depleted and the replacement of which is very uncertain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is only for excess profits tax purposes.
This is a half-way measure, but I am thankful for it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is more than half way.
Does resolution 31 cover more than one taxation period? Does it cover, perhaps or possibly, three taxation periods?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not stated, and frankly I am not sure about it. That will be indicated in the bill.

There is nothing to equate the amount of expenditure which may be made in the future with the actual amount of deferred maintenance and repairs. Take the railways, for instance. It was stated by the Canadian National in the railway committee- of course this company is not subject to taxation and does not come under the Minister of National Revenue-that they have set aside a large amount of money for deferred maintenance. I questioned them as to how they arrived at the amount and I was informed that
Income War Tax

they had made an actual physical survey of how many stations would have been painted had the paint and labour been available, and how much work on the various sections of the line would have been done. They had made an accurate accounting computation of deferred maintenance, and I believe last year they set aside $13,000,000 for that particular purpose. How will the department know that under this provision full compensation will be made the deferred maintenance? With some concerns it might work out satisfactorily, while with others it might not. I can see where it might be necessary to carry forward these provisions for two or three years in order that a plant might be able to make adequate maintenance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would be impossible for the department to say that an actual expenditure made by a company, let us say in 1945, represented ten per cent deferred maintenance and ninety per cent maintenance for that year. We assume that some repairs are being made all the time, and it is recognized that the average concern cannot do full repairs or make full maintenance. They will catch up on these, presumably, as soon as men and materials are available. This resolution provides that the actual expenditure incurred after a date to be fixed may be charged, one-half to a back period and be considered, arbitrarily, if you will, as the cost of deferred maintenance, and the remaining half to be charged as current expense. I am afraid I cannot give any other explanation than that.

While this resolution does give some relief where there has been overtaxation on income which was not true income, it leaves out entirely the cost of reconversion. Because of the war and to some extent because of the length of it, I suppose well over fifty per cent of the industries of this country are being used to a greater or less degree on war production. In some cases their whole layout has been changed completely to produce munitions of war, and their peacetime production has fallen by the wayside. There is no provision here to cover the cost of reconversion, nor do I see any in any other resolution. I believe that the cost of reconverting a plant which has been on war production should be properly chargeable to war profits, just as we are doing in the case of deferred maintenance, which is chargeable to years in which the money was not spent and in which the over-taxation has taken place. One of the most important questions in connection with post-war matters is the cost of reconversion, which leaves a man's plant in no better condition than it was in 1939 or when he first turned his energies to war production. With the ter-

mination of the war his contracts end and he is faced with the problem of reconverting in order that he may once more turn out goods for civilian consumption. In some plants this cost will run into hundreds of thousands of dollars. In many small plants it will bt $10,000 or $20,000, which is a considerable item. I believe the revenue department should give the same consideration to this problem as they have given to the question of deferred maintenance and repairs.
I should like to hear from the parliamentary assistant if there are any good reasons to the contrary. I have talked over this matter with some industrialists who are going to be faced with this problem, and they find themselves short of working capital because they have paid out so much in taxes to the government and have not been allowed to accumulate any reserves for this purpose. I think one could say that they are at their wits' end to know how they are going to finance the cost of reconversion. If there could be some tax relief it would help in a small measure to solve the problem with which they are going to be faced, namely, the providing of employment through civilian production.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that this problem of reconversion is one to which the government will have to give, and is giving now to some extent, the most careful consideration. However, reconversion costs are primarily capital costs. Repairs and maintenance have always been recognized in income tax law as current operating expenses. The cost of reconverting a plant has always been recognized as a capital expense and would be charged as such on the books of the company, would be set up as a capital charge and be subject to depreciation. In a great many war plants a substantial amount of capital cost will have been written off during the war by virtue of accelerated depreciation or by a combination of accelerated depreciation and ordinary depreciation. I do not want to minimize the importance of this reconversion problem or to be understood as saying that it is not one to which the government should give consideration, perhaps consideration in framing a budget, although I feel, or rather I hope, that it is a matter which could be more appropriately dealt with in the next budget rather than this one. It is primarily a capital matter and involves questions of high government policy as to how these plants are to be reconverted.

We have the government already giving consideration to the Industrial Development bank, which might very well be left to a subsequent session if brought up at all. I admit the distinction between capital

Income War Tax
assets and what can properly be charged to maintenance and repairs, but the parliamentary assistant said that most of these war plants had allowances through which they could write off their capital assets which were devoted to war purposes. That is a rightful provision, for the owners of these plants have created certain assets for the production of war materials which will be of little or no use after the war, and the writing off of that capital expenditure should take place during the war. But the parliamentary assistant has endeavoured to hang the principle of exclusion of reconversion costs from this section on to the idea that reconversion has to do with capital assets and that the company can spend its money on rebuilding its plant and getting it ready for civilian production and charge the cost off to depreciation.
But in the great majority of cases a company which has been in war production and has written off its war production facilities, which are now in many cases completely useless, has to use the same physical space to recreate capacity for producing civilian goods, and therefore the company is not better off now than it was in 1939. The company fihds that it has to spend a great deal of money in the way of capital, if you want to call it capital, to put itself in the position in which it was before the war. Some allowance should be made for this expenditure, which will amount to a great deal in the case of many companies, many of them without working capital. Relief, or the promise of relief, should be given to them in the present budget and not in some future one. If the parliamentary assistant's reasoning about postponing the matter to a future budget carries any weight at all, the Industrial Development bank should also be postponed until then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Not at all. That is setting
up a piece of machinery.
It is for the very purpose *of reconverting war assets into civilian assets.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Only in part. That is one of the reasons but by no means the only one.

It is the chief reason that gives the thing any commendation whatsoever. There is no use in having committees and commissions to investigate post-war possibilities and reconstruction problems, such as the James commission and others which the government has created on the principle that the government believes in private enterprise, when at the same time the government will not restore the motivating force behind private [DOT] enterprise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Surely the hon. member does not suggest that we should reduce taxation at this stage of the war.

The parliamentary assistant is always bringing up the question of reducing taxation. The hon. member for Parry Sound said that it takes at least four years to bring a gold mine into production from the time of the initial strike, and similarly I say that it takes business a considerable time to lay its plans, to reconvert its plant for civilian production and to recreate markets for its civilian goods which will be needed after the war. All this takes a great amount of work and money. The parliamentary assistant says that we can discuss this matter in the next budget a year from now. By that time we shall have many more men discharged from the services who will be looking for employment. Already we have 150,000 discharged, and we hope that within the next six months we shall have more men discharged than there are jobs immediately available. It is high time therefore that the ground work of industry should be laid so that we may have post-war employment for these men who will be returning.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury)There is one observation I should make arising out of a remark made to my colleague by the parliamentary assistant. He said: "Surely you are not suggesting that we should reduce taxation at the present time." I say, Mr. Chairman, that this budget is reducing taxation. Some of these proposals are reducing taxation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Very little.
But the principle is there. So that the statement made by the parliamentary assistant is not correct.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are merely adjusting some inequalities.

You are wiping out some taxation in this budget as well as making adjustments. We are suggesting reductions in taxation, and the reductions which were suggested in our amendment were evaluated by the minister as representing a large sum of money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Then let me correct my statement. Surely you are not suggesting substantial reductions in taxation at the present time.

We are suggesting reductions in taxation in order to meet the situation that will arise in the post-
Income War Tax

war period. I want to say this to the minister and he can tell it to his friends. The reductions in income taxation which the opposition- amendment advocated this year will not begin to equal the waste in the army in Canada, will not begin to equal the amount of money which the Department of National Defence is wasting in the army in Canada. That is my answer to the statement of the parliamentary assistant.

I represent an industrial district, Mr. Chairman, and I do not like the wording of resolution 31. I realize that when the tumult and the shouting dies and the captains and the kings depart in two or three weeks and when parliament will have prorogued, the budget resolutions which we are now passing will have a far different meaning in effect from what this high court of parliament now thinks. We shall make a very grave mistake if we pass this resolution as it stands. It says that one-half of the expenditures on maintenance and repairs incurred by any taxpayer carrying on a business in a period fixed by an order in council shall be regarded as deferred maintenance, and so forth. That includes trade and commerce, large and small businesses. But what did the Minister of Munitions and Supply say the other day? He said that you could not get materials and you could not get labour to do this specific repair and maintenance work. The resolution goes on to say that this provision shall apply also in the case of a taxpayer operating a mine. That is all right. I have always been one of those who ever since the war started have supported the development of our mining resources and all natural resources to furnish employment to our soldiers when they come back from the war, and I think public opinion will support that. But I object to the discrimination which this resolution makes against the small industrial business man. Let it be remembered that a very large proportion, forty-two per cent of our income tax revenue, comes from Ontario and the industrial income tax districts of Toronto.
I object to the language of this resolution. If we pass it as it is, we shall go home and then within two or three weeks the government can fix maintenance and repairs, deductions for expenses, the period and time and place, all by order in council. Already since the war started we have passed nearly 50.000 orders in council. We are fast approaching the stage where the word "liberty" will be meaningless in this country, because we are being governed right and left by rules and regulations, forms

and restrictions, passed under order in council. If you take resolutions 31 and section 33 together-because they are kindred resolutions -and all the resolutions from 20 to 29, you will find that everything that is an enactment is to be done over our heads by means of rules and regulations and instructions and other enactments issued through the department.
Ever since the start- of this war I have been objecting to the work of this red-tape factory that has been set up in the east block, where orders in council are passed and the government of the country has been handed over to various control boards No wonder the people are turning against the old parties. They are turning against those parties because parliament has divested itself of practically all its rights and privileges and has delegated all its functions to one control board after another. But that is the very thing that we are fighting against in this war.
The other day I had a letter from a small business man in my constituency, and he referred to what I said in 1942 in connection with this very same question. He wrote telling me that he would lose his small industrial business, the little store he had, and his home, as a result of income tax and the various restrictions by which business is being hampered. Not only that, but his boy, he said, would be deprived of that schooling to which he was entitled. This man fails to see the necessity for all these regulations.
This whole red-tape factory, in my opinion, should be abolished. We are simply handing over executive power to a bureaucracy, and we are doing it under resolutions 31 and 33. We are well on the road sooner or later to the totalitarian state. In England, in the late Sir Kingsley Wood's budget about two or three years ago there was a discussion similar to that which has been taking place here to-day, in connection with this income tax question, and several members made an argument very much along the lines of the argument advanced to-day by the hon. member for York-Sunbury and others. They referred at that time over there to the various abuses that have crept in as a result of the passing of all these orders in council, rules and regulations. In a remarkable pamphlet written two years ago, "Possible Recovery?" Dean Inge put the matter in a more definite way:
Our upper and middle classes^ in supporting this war committed suicide with their eyes open. They knew that at the end of it they would find themselves deprived of nearly the whole of their incomes, forced to surrender all the comforts and luxuries which their families had enjoyed, and -many of them driven from

Income War Tax
the homes which they had come to love. So great a sacrifice has never before been voluntarily made. I know of no other instance in which a whole class has deliberately signed its own death warrant. No doubt they had not much choice in the matter, since there is a constituency in which the taxpayers are more numerous than the tax-eaters.
He is referring in England to the pacifists' policy.
No doubt they had no suspicion that the stupidest government of modern times had committed them to a single-handed struggle against the greatest military power in the world. No doubt many of them believed that war was forced upon us. But their chivalry in laying down all that they had on .the altar of patriotism has not been sufficiently recognized.
I would not go as far as the Gloomy Dean, but it is obvious by now that a whole class, perhaps a predominating section of society, whether it has voluntarily committed suicide, or not, has been for practical purposes exterminated in the last four years by budgets. People cannot get labour or materials for any maintenance or repairs. On Yonge street the other day I saw small businessmen putting out their goods on the public street on a side lot. What is the reason for all this? Since the war started we have been virtually abolishing private ownership. In the days of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier everyone owned a little property of some sort, a small store or mill, * a cow, a team, a small truck, a grocery concern or something of that sort. But since the war started all this has been swept away by the action of parliament in placing artificial barriers and burdens on industry and in handing over power to boards of control. Three years ago in the British House of Commons, as result of pressure brought to bear upon the administration, they were forced to embody in the budget statute many of the rales and regulations that previously had been promulgated by order in council.
There are many inequalities, inconsistencies and injustices to the small businessman and the small manufacturer who pay income tax, and when we go home we shall be faced with a great deal of criticism. The taxpayers are up in arms as a result of what is now taking place. We have the highest income tax in the world, although it may be argued that it is not the highest exactly in that form. But in the United States and in England they have no sales tax as we have it here. Here, when you add the sales tax, corporation tax, excess profits tax, surtaxes and all other taxes the people have to pay, you find that we have the highest taxation in the world. No doubt the government needed the money for war purposes, and no one objects to that.
The ministry must have money, but there is a right way and there is a wrong way of getting that money. I know there is a great chorus of approval, in the press and over the radio, of the victory loan, and a great hip, hip, hurrah over this budget. But when hon. members go home let them talk to men and women in industry and they will find that there is not the same enthusiasm lor all this as we find on the part of this large regiment of paid officials, radio and press boosters, information bureau and all the others on whom we are spending something like a million dollars.
I should like to see this session conclude as quickly as possible, and the opposition has given a great deal of help to the government; but you will find that the people back home have more knowledge than we have of what is going to happen to them and the real meaning of it all as a result of all these orders in council and these rules and regulations.
We also need a vast housing and reconstruction policy1. With regard to reconstruction the minister forgot many things in the budgeb-materials, house building allowances, maintenance and repairs and a national housing plan. If there were allowances for housing and many other things like that in industry, construction and reconstruction, the people would not object to it. What were the industries engaged in this industry called housing told? They were told the other day by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that they could not get any materials or labour for that particular work, let alone any allowance along the lines indicated. When I was speaking on this matter two years ago I was told by the. minister that I was shooting holes through the budget.
I was not trying to shoot any holes through the budget. But the orders in council, the control boards, the rules and regulations and orders in council shoot holes through the budget, and they will do it to such an extent that we shall not know resolutions 31 and 33 when they are passed, and neither will the taxpayers. Instead of getting allowance for maintenance and all that kind of thing you will find that the applicant will be ruled out by a bureaucracy.
I have admiration and respect for the present minister's head of departments and the chief commissioner, but he has an intolerable task. I think it is the unanimous opinion of the committee and of the public generally that he is a most excellent officer. I think it would be far better for him in the administration of his work if he did not have to allow political machinery and orders in council
Income War Tax

to get beyond control, and if we did not allow this government to come along and pass orders in council or some rules and regulations which will entirely change these resolutions we pass, and make them mean something entirely different from what resolution 31 means.

On this
subject of reconversion I think the hon. member for Rosedale has done a real service in bringing up this topic. I for one regret that there is no intimation in the budget speech, and therefore none in the resolutions, dealing with the subject matter. I wonder if in certain industries which are no longer engaged in war work this problem has not already been facing the department. I would think that there must have been a number of cases where the position has been met and is now being dealt with in the tax situation. As I listened to the discussion between the parliamentary assistant and the hon. member for Rosedale, my mind led me to believe that theoretically and technically this would be a capital expenditure. I think scientifically that would be the correct category, and yet the suggestions that have been made to give some measure of relief apply with equal cogency for the allowance as it did for the capital expenditure in these plants for war purposes. I hope that consideration is being given to that position by the department, although I see nothing in the law as I understand it to-day which would allow it to be dealt with as a special problem. It strikes me that it is a special problem. I can only express the hope, without any thorough knowledge of the situation or the scientific principles upon which legislation should be based, that within a year, if not now-and I would hope now-consideration will be given to this problem and that equity and justice will be done.

This resolution includes
underground development in the case of mines, I believe?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.

Some of us have received
representations from people interested in mining. They put forward special recommendations for the taxing of the mining industry. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant has had some.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I have had quite a lot,
yes.

The officers of the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue are really in this position. They have in part the future of the whole mining industry of Canada in their hands. That is a condition

which has arisen by reason of the heavy taxation. I freely admit it is wrong that they should have that responsibility, but that actually is the position at the present time.
I ask the parliamentary assistant to make some comments on these recommendations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If I may interrupt, I do not know whether my hon. friend was in his place when the question came up a little earlier and I quoted the minister's reference to it in his budget speech at page 4183 of Hansard:
I have the minister's reference here. In effect the minister said that he hoped there would be a dominion-provincial conference and that everything would be lovely after that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think that is a fair paraphrase of what he said; it was a little more complete than that.
He did not go much farther than that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He pointed1 out concessions that have already been made to the mining industry and that it was premature until the dominion-provincial conference had been held to make any radical changes in tax policy applicable only to the mining and oil companies. I put the statement on Hansard.

I have it here. But I think the situation is sufficiently serious and the recommendations are sufficiently clear to justify some comment from the parliamentary assistant. The recommendations are as follows:
That depletion allowance of fifty per cent of the net earnings of metal and industrial mineral *mines be allowed, and extended to dividends paid by suoh mines.
That taxes paid annually to provincial governments and to municipalities be allowed as a deduction from earnings of all mining companies before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax purposes.
That all annual expenditures made by mining companies on outside exploration in any part of Canada, excepting cost of options or purchase of property, be allowed as a deduction from earnings before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax.
The statement goes on to point out:
The above recommendations represent unanimous views of all investigating bodies appointed by government and industry alike as to the proper method of providing an overall equitable plan of mining taxation and to place the industry on a footing where it will best be able to perpetuate itself to the lasting benefit of Canada.
Some point is also made of the fact that even though those changes are not made now it will be very helpful if the government will announce their policy of mining taxation for

Income War Tax
the post-war years. That would enable men interested in mining to make the necessary preparations now so that they could go ahead and develop their mines after the war. I think the parliamentary assistant will agree that it would be beneficial if the mining industry could have some such blueprint as that. Would he make some comment on these recommendations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Along with other hon. members I received a great many of these recommendations. The minister also received them prior to the preparation of the budget and prior to the deliver}' of his budget speech. There is really nothing that I can add to what he said at page 4182 of Hansard with respect to the consideration given to the taxing of the mining industry. He refrained from dealing with these specific recommendations. It is true that he dealt with the subject in a rather general fashion, but he did deal in some particular fashion with the special provisions already made for the mining industry from the tax point of view. I cannot speak for him, but my feeling is that it is premature at this stage of the war to attempt to revise the taxation structure for the mining industry alone. I think it has to be dealt with in a larger picture by revising our tax structure when the war is over or so nearly over that we know what our commitments are going to be. I personally do not believe that we can now single out the mining industry as a special industry for special concessions other than the ones which are already contained in the act. I think it should be dealt with as the minister said-and I am only paraphrasing it-as a part of an integrated plan for the taxing of all industry and business. I would not be prepared to comment on these specific suggestions; and, speaking generally, that is the reply which I have given to a number of people who have written me personal letters putting forward these suggestions.
Then in effect the government will make no announcement regarding these recommendations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think the government can make any announcement now. My hon. friend suggested that no matter if we could not carry it out now, we should announce what our policy is going to be six or nine months from now.
No, I did not say six or nine months; I said for the post-war period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Well, I should say that would be at least six or nine months from now. It is pretty difficult to announce what your fiscal policy is going to be post-war until you
know what your commitments are going to be post-war. From a budgetary point of view I think it would be dangerous, to say the least, to attempt to put forward any specific proposals now, untij you know how long the war is going to last and what further effort will have to be put forth purely from a war point of view. I think it is too soon.
Sooner or later the dominion government will have to decide on a plan, and I do not think it will get much help through holding a dominion-provincial conference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This mining question is
certainly a matter on which it is essential that a dominion-provincial conference should be held, because the provinces are vitally interested in these mines. They come under the head of property and civil rights.
But the dominion is doing the taxing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is a joint matter; the provinces get substantial revenues from the mines, too.

Then what is the present position with regard to each of these three suggestions? For example, what is the position with regard to the depletion allowance and also with regard to the dividends paid by mines?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You are asking now for information?
They are asking for a fifty per cent depletion allowance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You are asking with respect to mines? A depletion of 33^ per cent is allowed now; and with respect to dividends paid by the mining companies, the recipients may deduct 20 per cent as not being taxable.

The second recommendation is that the taxes paid annually to provincial governments and municipalities be allowed as a deduction from earnings of all mining companies before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax purposes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All taxes paid to provincial and municipal governments are now allowed as a deduction, with exception of income taxes, and since income taxes are collected only by the federal government-
I think the hon. gentleman is wrong there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Taxes paid to provincial governments, other than income or profits taxes, are allowed as a deduction from gross mining revenues, as an expense. I am advised,



Income War Tax
and as a matter of fact I know from my own experience, that this is an absolutely accurate statement of the law.
What about municipal taxes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are allowed on the same basis.

The next recommendation is that all annual expenditures made by mining companies on outside exploration in any part of Canada, except the cost of options or purchase of property, be allowed as a deduction from earnings before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is covered by section 8(9) of the Income War Tax Act, which reads:
A corporation whose chief business is that of mining or exploring for metalliferous and strategic minerals shall be entitled to deduct from the sum total of the income tax payable by it under this act and the tax payable under the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, twenty-six and two-thirds per centum of all prospecting, exploration and development expenses incurred by it in searching for base metals and strategic metals during the period from the first day of January, 1943, to the thirty-first day of March, 1945: Provided, however, that such deduction must be taken against .the said taxes payable in respect of the year or fiscal period in which the said expenses -were actually incurred.
There is also a further proviso.
Does that apply to all mining companies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It applies to all mining companies, but only with respect to expenses incurred in the search for metalliferous and strategic minerals. Therefore it would not include expenses incurred in the search for gold.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
32. That the provision allowing deductions by a corporation from income of amounts paid by way of donations to charitable organizations in Canada be amended to provide that the amount of the donations made in excess of the average of the taxpayer's donations in the last two fiscal periods ending before July 1, 1942, shall be allowed as a deduction for purposes of the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, only to the extent that the total taxes payable by the taxpayer under the said acts are thereby diminished by forty per centum of the said excess, unless made before February 1, 1944, and paid or evidenced in writing before the said date or evidenced by a payment before the said date which is one of a series of payments to be made thereafter and accompanied by proper evidence of the undertaking.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I will ask that this resolution be allowed to stand until eight o'clock, when
[Mr. Abbott.)
the minister will be here. I believe he has some comments he wants to make in regard to it.
Resolution stands.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
