speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: 1.	That expenditures in respect of scientific research directly or indirectly related to the taxpayer's business, whether of a current or capital nature, be allowed as a deductible expense, in the case of expenditures of a current nature, in the year when the expenditures are made and, in the case of expenditures of a capital nature, over a three-year period commencing with the year of expenditure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is in substantially the same terms as the corresponding resolution under the Income War Tax Act. The committee will recall that resolution 23 under the Income War Tax Act provides that expenditures for scientific research and the like are treated as an expense, and a similar provision is to be inserted in the Excess Profits Tax Act.
Is there any definition of what constitutes scientific research, or is it left to the discretion of the minister?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think that is being worked out and will appear in the bill when it is brought down. I do not know that the drafting is quite complete yet.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
2.	That in the computation of capital employed for the taxation year and subsequent periods the requirement to reduce capital by one-half of the dividends paid in cash during any taxation year be altered to provide that such reduction shall be made only -to the extent that earned surplus at the end of the taxation year is less than earned surplus at the beginning of the year.
The hon. gentleman might give us an explanation of this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In effect this resolution
proposes a technical amendment to the definition of "capital employed". Hon. members will recall that under the law as it now

Excess Profits Tax
stands "capital employed" is defined to include paid-up capital and surplus as it stood at the end of the base period, which I think is December 31, 1939, or the last fiscal period in 1939. The law now provides that this figure of capital employed should be reduced by one-half the dividends paid in cash during the taxation period.
They are to be deducted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: One-half of the dividends paid during the taxation period are to be deducted from the total capital employed, or from the figure as defined under the act as being the capital employed. The proposed amendment provides that if the earned surplus at the end of a fiscal period subsequent to the standard period is not less than at the beginning of the period, notwithstanding the payment of dividends, the capital will remain at the same figure. In other words, if a company pays its dividends entirely out of current earnings, its capital employed, for the purpose of determining standard profits, will not be reduced by one-half of the dividends paid during the year.
That is very fair. If they are paid out of surplus the capital will be reduced?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
Which section of the act does that amend?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Section 4 of the first
schedule of the Excess Profits Tax Act.
Was that schedule passed by this house, or is it in the regulations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is part of the statute. I have the section before me, and perhaps it would help the committee if I read it:
Capital as hereinbefore defined shall be increased or decreased by a portion of any bona fide additions to or reductions of the assets of the business made during the taxation period other than additions or reductions resulting from profits or losses of the said period, such increase or decrease to be made pro rata for the time such additions were employed in or decreases withdrawn from the business, provided however, that dividends paid in cash during such period shall constitute a deduction from the capital employed at the commencement at the said period to the extent of one-half the total amount of dividends paid during the same period.
The effect of this proposed amendment will be that if payment of those dividends does not result in reducing the earned surplus as it
100-319i
stood at the beginning of the period, there will be no reduction in the amount of capital employed.
That is fair.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
3. That the refundable portion in respect of which a taxpayer is entitled to repayment may in case of bankruptcy, liquidation, winding-up or dissolution, be repaid in accordance with regulations made by the governor in council.

This resolution deals with payments made in certain cases of bankruptcy, liquidation, winding-up or dissolution. It states that the refundable portion to which a taxpayer is entitled shall be repaid in accordance with the regulations made by the governor in council. The money is taxpayers' money. If it is a corporation which goes into bankruptcy, liquidation, winding-up or dissolution it is proposed to return it to the taxpayer or to the trustee in bankruptcy, or the liquidator, or as we call it in my part of the country, the curator. On dissolution it would be returned to the shareholders. There would be a distribution of the assets of the corporation.
What has the administration in mind with respect to limitation on this? In the case of bankruptcy this money belongs to the creditors, we will say. I think that is correct, although I am afraid a substantial amount of it would go to the costs of liquidation. In liquidation it may or may not go to the creditors, depending on the kind of liquidation, and the reasons therefor.
I think the resolution is too scanty. The question I would put to the parliamentary assistant would be this: What has the government in mind with respect to regulations to be made in each or all of these circumstances?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I can answer it in this way. My hon. friend will appreciate the difficulty which has arisen in respect of a few companies which have either been liquidated, or their charters surrendered. Some of those companies had on their books a refundable portion of the tax, which was an asset. But of course that is not payable, as the law now stands, until after the cessation of hostilities.
The question arose as to who should hold it, to whom it should be paid, and who is entitled to receive it. The liquidator might wish to get his discharge. I think it was ruled, rightly or wrongly, that if a company wound up and the liquidator was discharged, the right to receive the refundable portion was gone. That did not seem equitable. On
Excess Profits Tax

the other hand it was felt it should not be left to a departmental ruling as to what should be done with this money when it eventually became payable. I would welcome any suggestions any hon. members may have. However, it was suggested, after consideration, that power be vested in the governor in council to approve regulations. In other words, it is put on a little more formal basis than a mere departmental ruling. A formal order in council would have to be passed setting up rules providing for the retaining of this money in the meantime or, perhaps, paying it over under certain safeguards, placing it in escrow or something like that. The situation which it is intended to correct is that the right to receive this deferred amount should not be lost .to creditors or shareholders, as the case may be. It is merely a question of setting up the proper machinery.
I suppose situations have arisen which demand the recognition of some action. That must be the cause of its being here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Correct.

I suggest that in the case of bankruptcy this money should not be kept; it should go to the creditors. Why should it be kept in escrow or kept with the government for a period of time, when the shareholders have not received it? They should get it immediately. I would hope that principle would prevail.
On the other end of the equation is the question of dissolution. The dissolution of a company usually takes place when the shareholders want to go out of business, and surrender their charter. They pay off all their liabilities to the public, and have only liabilities to their own shareholders. They convert their assets into cash, and distribute those assets among the shareholders pro rata. But they cannot distribute this refundable portion. What has the administration in mind with respect to that? Is that going to be held? It is not quite as pressing a problem as that connected with bankruptcy. That would be recognized.
I have an open mind as to what should be done in a case of that kind, although I realize that companies do not dissolve unless their usefulness is pretty well over, or a proprietor wants to get out of business because of age, or for some like reason. It might be a hardship if this were kept from them, although their estates would of course take it, as in the case of deceased persons.
The other two classes are in between the two extremes, as I understand it. The minister has given us the reason why this has

been brought down now, but he has not followed the whole picture through. What does he propose to do in the case of a dissolution by a company?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Of course, I do not know
that that is fully settled. My hon. friend will appreciate the difficulties here. His suggestion that in the case of 'bankruptcy it might be in the public interest to pay money to the creditors at the time the assets are being distributed is perhaps a good one, although we have to remember that these refundable portions do not bear interest.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Therefore the taxpayer who gets it back now, or at an early date, would have an advantage over the shareholders, let us say, of a company which continues in operation. There must be some safeguard against that. It would not be fair, for instance, to allow a small, privately held company voluntarily to wind up and surrender its charter, all the shareholders then being able to get their pro rata portion of the refundable portion.
The thought was that perhaps it would be desirable to try to work out a set of regulations covering these cases. This presumably will be a temporary condition; it will not last in perpetuity. Those regulations should be approved by order in council, and that should be the code, as it were, to govern the disposition of refundable portions in these cases. None of the creditors is really entitled to demand his money now It is to make some provision for the holding of the money during the period of transition.

Does not
the parliamentary assistant think that the creditors stand in a slightly different position from that of the shareholders?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should think so, yes.

I think
they ought to be given more consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I think so, yes; I should
think consideration should be given to that.

However,
we will wait and see. This just gives power to make regulations, and it will not be revealed, even *when the bill comes down, as to what the regulations are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
But if it is done by order in council, the order in council would be tabled. It would be public. I think it is perhaps a little difficult to expect that this should be spelled out in the statute now. It is a matter which it seems to me might safely be

Excess Profits Tax
left to disposition by regulation, with the added safeguard that it has to be approved by order in council, rather than by just a departmental regulation. However, I have an open mind in the matter.

I am not in accord with the general principle underlying the statement just made. I think as far as possible regulations dealing with the money of the taxpayers of this country should be brought down and revealed to the world in the enabling legislation that is to be passed

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would agree with that as a general principle.

Once again I wish to voice my protest against government by regulation, against taxation by regulation and now against the distribution of the taxpayers' money by regulation. I am not going to follow the point farther than that, but I think the principle is bad.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that this is being done to give some relief.

This is another example of the uncertainty which attaches to refundable taxes. Something the same was found to exist in connection with the refundable taxes of individuals. The government found that to be unworkable because it was not understandable, largely because of the uncertainty. I can understand why it was not possible to make the refundable portion of the individual's tax negotiable, namely his receipt or whatever evidence he might have, but what objection could there be to making the refundable part of the corporation tax negotiable so that it might be transferred from one company to another and thus obviate some of the difficulty which this resolution indicates may exist?
I understand that if a company sells its assets it cannot sell its right to the refundable portion of its taxes because that refundable portion attaches to the charter itself. This creates a certain amount of difficulty for a company endeavouring to dispose of its assets. Would the parliamentary assistant explain why the refundable taxes owing to a corporation cannot be made negotiable? If someone is willing to buy at eighty or eighty-five per cent of the value and a corporation wishes to sell, it is of no concern of any one but the corporation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I must confess that I find it difficult to see any difference between compulsory savings owing to an individual and compulsory savings in the case of a company.

The company cannot
spend them and force up prices as an individual may do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I still cannot see why we should make a distinction between the two.

If an individual has three or four hundred dollars in refundable taxes coming to him and can negotiate these at the bank or with another individual and get the money, he can spend it, but I do not see how the same principle can be applied to a corporation. If a corporation wants more money very likely it can go to the bank and get it and then spend it, if desired. If the refundable taxes owing to corporations were made negotiable this whole difficulty would be got away from.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: So far as I know this is the first time this point has been raised. It was considered desirable that a company should have a reserve available in the form of these refundable portions for the reconversion purposes, let us say, about which my hon. friend was talking a little earlier. These reserves may not be adequate in all cases, but they will certainly be a help to many companies in effecting reconversion. If you make them assignable or transferable a company, in order to realize on its assets, may sell them to some other company. Frankly I am thinking aloud, because this question has not been raised before to my knowledge. I cannot see offhand why there should be any special distinction between the individual and the corporation.
The right of assignment is dealt with in what resolution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the next resolution.

I asked a banker recently if a bank would lend money on an assignment or hypothecation of a refundable portion, and he said, "Certainly not because the time of payment is too remote and uncertain." But he told me it would be accepted as collateral security on the borrower's own note. I do not think this is of much benefit to business, but at the same time it is some alleviation. Consideration might be given to paying the actual cash in cases where a company finds itself in a difficult position in the reconversion period.
These companies want certainty; they want something they can depend upon. I do not wish to labour the point, but I think this money which does not bear interest, which belongs to the taxpayer, which in effect is a
Excess Profits Tax

forced loan without interest, should be made available to him according to his requirements at the earliest possible day.

Why cannot some consideration be given by the department to putting some maturity on the refundable portions which are paid under the 1944 tax? They could be made to mature three or four years hence in order that business may have some certainty. I am not suggesting doing anything about the refundables which have already been created. But if you made them mature in a reasonable period you would give business some certainty as to what it has. This would create collateral against which business could borrow for reconversion and reconstruction purposes. It would also be good collateral in the hands of the banks. You have gone a long way for the individual, possibly because you could not sell him the idea, and here you have the same situation with regard to industry. If these were made repayable in three or four years, or in whatever time the minister thinks the war will be over, there would be greater certainty and there would be the possibility of greater use for refinancing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Under section 18, subsection 2 of the Excess Profits Tax Act the maturity is fixed with respect to the refundable portions in the different years. In the case of 1942 it will be the second fiscal period commencing after the cessation of hostilities; in the case of 1943, it will be the third fiscal period after the cessation of hostilities, and so on. Then there is the further provision that notwithstanding the provisions of the sections to which I have referred, they may mature at such earlier times and in such instalments as the governor in council may determine. The outside limit of the maturity is fixed and the government may anticipate that maturity.

It was impossible for the individual to understand the law with regard to the refundable portion of his tax, and it took five or six lines of highly legal language to explain it. It may be you have made things a little clearer here, but if you could state a definite year it would be much better.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
4. That the refundable portion in respect of which a taxpayer is entitled to repayment may be assigned by way of security in cases where the governor in council is satisfied that the purpose of the assignment is to enable the taxpayer to make capital expenditures that will contribute to the post-war conversion of the taxpayer's business and will provide substantial employment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is a comment I should like to make in connection with this resolution. There is a principle here which

it seems to me is good. In fact, if my memory serves me correctly, it is a principle that was advocated in this corner some time ago when the Excess Profits Tax Act was put upon the statute books. I refer to the responsibility of the government to see to it that the refundable portion of the excess profits taxes is used for post-war reconstruction and the provision of employment, in the postwar period. I believe that from this group a few years ago the proposal was made that all of the twenty per cent when refunded should be earmarked for those purposes. Now we have in this resolution the acceptance to a limited extent of that principle. By limited extent I mean that it applies only to those who are able to liquidate their refundable portion in advance by the methods set out in the resolution. In cases where taxpayers, corporations, are able to do that under the terms of this resolution, they are called upon to meet the government's requirements that the money be used for post-war conversion of their business and to provide substantial employment. I repeat that that is good. But it seems to me that if it is good for those taxpayers who will be able to liquidate their refundable portion in advance in this way, it is -an equally good principle for all. I know my hon. friends to my right will probably say again, as they have said several times this afternoon, that this is the corporate taxpayer's money, but I would remind them that this is excess profit and that this profit is due to the war, and we feel that the tax on the excess profit should go right up to 100 per cent. Since however, the government has made provision for the return of twenty per cent I think the idea that the government should direct, to some extent at least, the use of that twenty per cent is a good one, but if it is being done under the terms of this resolution 1 suggest that there ought to be legislation to do likewise with the refundable portion in all cases.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This is a very limited right which is given. It is not desired that any one taxpayer should be able to get his refundable portion ahead of another. But in special cases if a taxpayer is able to borrow money which he proposes to use for capital expenditures which will contribute to the postwar conversion of his business, the governor in council may authorize the assignment of his claim to the refundable portion as security for that advance. Three parties are involved- the taxpayer, the lender and the crown. It is a soft of three-cornered arrangement. I do not know how much it will be availed of. Obviously the lender, if he advances money

Income War Tax
against the claim, can take an out-and-out assignment on a discount basis because it does not bear interest, or he might take it as collateral security. I think the average case might be where a business might want to expend money to reconvert its war plant to a peace plant. It has a reasonable credit standing and also some accumulated refundable portion of the tax. If it were able to assign that as security to a lender, it might be able to get a loan which it might not otherwise be able readily to obtain. But the governor in council would have to be satisfied that the money was to be used for the postwar conversion of the taxpayer's business.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I emphasize the last few words that the parliamentary assistant used. Even with the other conditions which have been set out it will be necessary under this resolution, for the corporate taxpayer to satisfy the authorities that its purpose is to do a certain amount of post-war conversion and to provide employment. All I am doing at this point is to emphasize that that is a good principle, and I hope that it will be remembered.

I should like to ask if the procedure that will be adopted has been worked out. A taxpayer wants to make a capital expenditure for reconversion purposes. I would assume that he would have to file some sort of petition or brief with the department asking for permission to assign the refundable portion to a creditor who will presumably advance money against it, whether by way of total assignment or hypothecation or lien. Then I assume that the taxpayer will have to show that he will provide substantial employment. Just what procedure will be adopted? What are all the factors that will enable him to do that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That has not yet all been worked out. This is an enabling measure, but the procedure will, I think, be very much as the hon. gentleman has indicated. An industry that "had a project in mind and wanted this assistance would file a brief with the Department of Finance or some other department.
That is what I wanted to know. Under whose jurisdiction would it be?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It will be the Department of National Revenue, I would think. If the department is satisfied on the facts as presented, the minister would submit a recommendation to council authorizing the assignment, and I take it that an agreement would be entered into. I am only speculating because the procedure has not yet been worked out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on resolution 32.

In the course of the remarks I made on the budget on July 3 I adverted to this proposal which we now have concretely before us. So far as I can see, there is no mention of this proposal in the minister's budget statement. I think that is correct. But the basis of the remarks I made on July 3 was contained in a press release, which unfortunately I have not before me, made by the minister just prior to the opening of parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just to keep the record straight-
I am not sure about my time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -I made the statement in parliament first. In fact, I made two statements, one at the end of January and one about the middle of February, and nothing was given to the press before parliament met. Anything given to the press was given after I made a statement in the house.

It seems I am entirely wrong, and I am depending only on my memory; but I had the idea that notice had been given to the public that the provisions of the last budget, the laws relating to gifts to charitable and educational institutions, would not be allowed to come into effect. When the statement was made is a matter of minor importance. At any rate, I felt that was doing a grave injustice to a body of institutions in the country which are not simply charitable institutions, but which in this war have proven themselves to be a strong arm of government. I venture to assert that the work of certain of our educational institutions directly relating to the war has been of great and paramount importance for which probably some of them at all events have received wholly inadequate compensation. One of these institutions which
Income War Tax

I have in mind has given over its whole curriculum to the navy. I refer to King's college, Halifax, which has been taken over by the department of naval services, and is now a naval school of some kind, and for which the department is paying a rental of $30,000 per annum. I was going to say that the entire college population had to be transferred to Dalhousie university, and that added a great weight to that institution. No one is complaining about that. It was evidence of a measure of good will on the part of the authorities of the institution that does them nothing but honour and credit. The same is true of other institutions.
But the minister announced at some stage that the law as passed by parliament, because of developments which came as a result, would not be allowed to become operative, and in that I consider there was a breach of faith not only with the parliament of Canada and with the taxpaying public, but more particularly with the educational institutions of the country. I deplore that attitude on the part of the government because it must have known, when the law was made as it was, that a substantial part of the excess profits tax which is given to charitable and educational institutions would come out of taxation. That was abundantly clear at the very beginning. I assume that when the minister learned that advantage was being taken by these institutions of the position and used the taxing position, the legal position, as an inducement to corporations within the excess profits tax clause to make contributions, he must have known that those in the 100 per cent class would be taking that money out of taxation, except, I suppose, the twenty per cent refundable which ultimately would come out of the taxpayer. I deplored that position in the statement I made in the house on July 3 in discussing the budget.
I am not going to cover the same ground again; I think that would be a work of supererogation. I merely make these introductory remarks to explain that I was greatly perturbed by that position taken by the Minister of Finance as it affected certain educational institutions of the country, one or two of which are very dear to me and in whose prosperity and welfare I am intensely interested. Campaigns had been put on by the educational institutions, notably I believe by McGill, under which large sums of money in cash and in-pledges were given to some of these institutions, to be payable in cash or over a period of time, and which would have the taxation effect to which I have referred.
(Mr. R. B. Hanson.]
The effect of the minister's announcement was
absolutely to kill the efforts that were being made on behalf of these institutions whose corporate resources needed replenishing, and I thought and still think that was a reprehensible position for the minister to take, because the policy under which that became operative was the government's considered policy.
There was a time when a taxpayer could give up to ten per cent of his taxable income to education and charity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And still can.

That is for individuals; that is quite true. But under the Excess Profits Tax Act, if I apprehend the position of the law correctly, only five per cent could be given in the way I have indicated, and it is out of that that these gifts were made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The five per cent applies to corporations.

Well, it was from the corporations principally that these benefactions were expected to come, and it had the effect, at least until the position was fully clarified, of stopping any flow of donations to that class of institutions. I think that was a deplorable situation, and it is up to the minister to support his position.
I do not know that I have made the position absolutely clear, but I know what the effect is. The minister is making in effect what is retroactive legislation. In actual technical expression it may not be retroactive legislation, but it has the effect of being retroactive. It withdraws the provisions of the law as they have existed up to the present time and it substitutes a new formula. If I understand the position correctly-and I shall be glad to be corrected if I am wrong-it now provides that the amount of the donations made in excess of the average of the taxpayers' donations in the last two fiscal periods ending before July 1, 1942, shall be allowed as a deduction for purposes of the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act only to the extent that the total taxes payable by the taxpayer under the said acts are thereby diminished by forty per cent of the said excess, unless made before February 1, 1944, and paid or evidenced in writing before that date. That is a rather involved formula unless one studies it; but it is as clear as daylight to me.
I said this once before; it means a definite reduction in the amount that this class of taxpayer may give to charitable institutions under the tax-free clause, if that is the proper designation. I venture to suggest that there

Income War Tax
will be no further benefactions, no further contributions to education from that source. The average of such donations made by corporations within the excess profits clause in the two fiscal periods before July 1, 1942, was, I am informed, exactly nothing, or in most cases was absolutely nothing. Perhaps it is not wise to be too sweeping in this statement. It was little or nothing. I shall put it in that way. Therefore in most cases the amount that will now be allowed will be little or nothing. I think that is a very bad situation. There is no class of institution in this country which is feeling the pinch of war in its finances more than the smaller educational institutions, especially those that I know something about in the maritime provinces. They find their classes depleted; they find their revenues from tuition and what-not depleted. They have been doing a lot of good war work. They anticipate throwing the whole of their resources behind the government of the country in the post-war period in doing their share. The educational authorities are among the best class of citizens we have in this country. Yet when the opportunity for them to strengthen their .position at the expense, we will say, of the treasury presented itself, after the position was fully reviewed by the taxing authorities and the finance department of this country with their eyes wide open, as part of government policy, the government withdrew the privilege which those institutions thought they were going to enjoy, with the result that their hopes have been frustrated. That is putting it pretty mildly.
I suggest to the minister that he might have allowed at least one year's operation of this law. I know that in certain cases he would have lost substantial amounts of revenue. I think that is apparent. In the case of one institution which I mentioned, I believe that the sum of $7,000,000 was either paid in or will be paid in, evidenced by pledges in writing which will no doubt be redeemed, and that there will be substantial loss of revenue. But that is not the case of the smaller institutions which stand to suffer most. When the minister comes to make his statement, as of course he will, I want him to justify fully and on ethical grounds the reason for the change that he has made, because I cannot bring myself to believe that he is on strong and sound ground there. It does look to me-I hesitate to say this again; I said it pretty strongly on July 3-as though there were some breach of faith with the smaller institutions, and they certainly feel as I feel about it. They have not asked me to say this, but I know exactly their feelings. They have a sense of frustration in their endeavours to strengthen their position while they are doing a magnificent piece of war work. Anything and everything that the government has asked them to do they have done, and many of them without compensation. That cannot be said of some of the larger institutions. I know of one institution which has received from the army sums in excess of a million dollars in a single year. I should not say "I know", because I have not a personal knowledge, but I have been told that they have received sums in excess of a million dollars in a year. Some others have been paid and some have not been compensated for the services they have rendered.
I suggest to the minister that at this time an educational institution is one arm of government in Canada. It is not a charitable institution. I am not going to labour the point. I know the minister will put this thing through. He has announced he will .put it through. I suppose I am like the famous Bolivar. I am ploughing in the sands when I endeavour to get the minister to change his mind, because I have found he was inflexible in days gone by. But I could hardly let this opportunity go by without entering my protest against this type of legislation and against this change of policy on the part of the administration.

I had started to speak on resolution 32 this afternoon when it was allowed to stand. I wish to refer to the effect it has had on those who had a little money and had it taken away from them very largely by the burden of war and taxation. In everything that the minister does he has to get the money to run the war and support the war by income tax. About fifty-two per cent of the revenue comes from that source or from capital account. This resolution reads as follows:
That the provision allowing deductions by a corporation from income of amounts paid by way of donations to charitable organizations in Canada be amended to provide that the amount of the donations made in excess of the average of the taxpayer's donations in the last two fiscal periods ending .before July 1, 1942, shall be allowed as a deduction for purposes of the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, only to the extent that the total taxes payable by the taxpayer under the said acts are thereby diminished by forty per cent of the said excess, unless made before February 1, 1944, and paid or evidenced in writing before the said date or evidenced by a payment before the said date which is one of a series of payments to .be made thereafter and accompanied by proper evidence of the undertaking.	.
We are near the close of the fifth year of the war and, as hon. members know, our charitable organizations, the churches, the universities and colleges of this country have had a most

Income War Tax

precarious time of it. The same is true of the hospitals. As a result we were told the other day by the Department of Munitions and Supply that they had no materials, no labour to carry on this extensive building work in war time. The board of education of Toronto is many millions behind in primary and secondary schools. It has the money for it but has been refused materials and labour therefor.
Some constructive suggestions have been offered to the minister, among them a very good one coming from Archbishop Seager of the diocese of Huron, a gifted man, who is the metropolitan of the Church of England in Ontario, representing the house of bishops of the Church of England in Canada, supported by four other Protestant denominations, and also by Roman Catholic bodies and prominent members of their clergy. The bishop has written me several letters in the past nine or ten months. In the last one I received in May last he referred to the city of London, where they have a fine large university, Western, with a very fine medical faculty and some affiliated colleges. That university has done a great deal for western Ontario. Archbishop Seager wishes to offer some constructive suggestions to the minister, who, I believe, has had this memorandum laid before him. In his letter, Archbishop Seager says:
Locally, here in London, we of our own Huron college, together with the university of Western Ontario and the bishop of the Roman Catholic diocese of London have forwarded a proposal to the Minister of Finance in the shape of a memorandum, a copy of which I enclose. The essence of it is that subscriptions may continue to be made for actual building projects after the war, without being subject to any change in the regulations.
In addition, the university of Toronto is making its own representations in the matter . . .
There is a short preamble to the memorandum of this scholar and divine in which reference is made to the difficult time the universities and charitable organizations have had since the war began. As hon. members know, many of their sources of income have dried up on account of taxation and other economic controls, with the result that the universities, colleges and churches have been starved and the charitable organizations have been unable to carry on their work. I do not know what position they will be in after the war. We are a young country, of eleven and a half million people, and these charitable organizations, including the patriotic fund of the last war, the Red Cross, hospitals, churches, universities, and so on, all have to depend very largely upon private enterprise and private subscriptions from those who, before the present heavy taxes were imposed, gave mil-
IMr. Church ]
lions of dollars to these wonderful eharities and educational institutions of Canada. The preamble goes on to say:
The recent amendments to the Income Tax Act which narrow the limits of gifts corporations may make to institutions broadly classified as charitable, have so adversely affected the prospects of leading institutions in Canada as to arouse serious fears in the minds of their officers and governing boards. These fears touch at least two aspects of the national effort to draft, before the end of the war, definite and practicable plans of reconstruction (especially those bearing upon employment) for the first part of the post-war period. The administrators concerned are, with reason, genuinely apprehensive that the new restrictions, if left without modification, will entail certain deplorable results.
(1)	A large number of institutions which have already instituted specific construction projects and have succeeded in collecting a portion of the amounts needed, find their efforts brought practically to a standstill and their plans for taking their part in the activities of reconstruction defeated.
(2)	There is a real danger that the enforced failures to carry out projects as outlined in (1) constitute a great menace to the reconstruction plans of the government in regard both to the problem of unemployment and to the various kinds of social services which the institutions are designed to give.
Because of the government's declared desire to establish a sound and feasible policy of reconstruction in which all classes of citizens can cooperate, the following memorandum has been drawn up by representatives of educational and religious organizations of the dominion, in the hope that the government will give it careful consideration. It is asked that the memorandum be read in the light of the serious situation set forth in the foregoing preamble.
These representatives included four from the Protestant churches as well as some of the fine clergy of the Roman Catholic denomination, all united in the hope that the government will give the matter very careful consideration. The memorandum presented by this body is most constructive and helpful, and contains in the last clause a suggestion which I hope will be adopted. In substance it is as follows:
(a)	That the government, or the government's commission on reconstruction, institute a committee to be designated by some such title as the committee on approved building projects;
(b)	That the government request the educational and religious institutions to prepare plans for their respective building projects, and to submit such plans to the proposed committee on approved building projects;
(c)	That any such building project approved by the proposed committee be officially called an approved building project.
The proposers of this suggestion believe that once building plans have reached the stage of approval they can most expeditiously and economically be carried out by a responsible local committee of public-spirited, competent citizens.
Under the changes recently projected for the Income and Excess Profits Tax Acts, it seems that any corporation in Canada will not be per-

Income War Tax
mitted to charge as an expense operation more than the average of the donations made by that corporation during the two fiscal years ended prior to July 1, 1942, unless the corporation is willing to pay a tax of 60 per cent of the amount of the contribution exceeding the average of the two years above mentioned. Apparently no donations will be allowable which exceed the statutory limitations of the five per cent of the net earnings of the corporation.
It appears to be the expressed policy and intention of the government to carry out numerous construction projects following the war as a method of creating employment. In view of this fact the sponsors of this memorandum venture to suggest that the welfare of the Dominion of Canada and its citizens would be better served through the amendment to the Income War Tax Act, whereby the present stated policy of the government-that the average of the donations during the two fiscal years ended prior to July 1, 1942, shall not be exceeded by corporation donations to operating charitable funds-should be altered to permit a corporation to donate to approved construction projects the difference between the average of the two years above mentioned and five per cent of the net taxable income of the corporation, regardless of the possibility that the corporation might be subject to 100 per cent excess profits tax, and provided that all contributions received by the approved construction project committee must be invested in Dominion of Canada noninterest-bearing securities to be due and payable on a date six months after the cessation of hostilities.
In this connection one must bear this in mind: the costs of construction projects of the above character would be paid for by donations which, even though the corporations making them might be in the 100 per cent excess profits tax class, would represent in each ease a contribution of twenty per cent of shareholders funds which are repayable by the government to the corporation under the provision for refundable portion of the excess jjrofits tax as provided in the Excess Profits Tax Act. This proposed policy would remove the objection of the government to the diversion of funds which are very necessary for the prosecution of the war. It would also ensure that such funds would be received by the government in payment for noninterest-bearing securities, as proposed above, and provide that after the war the government refund twenty per cent of the excess profits tax to corporations. By virtue of the suggested amendment the amounts refunded would be devoted to special war reconstruction and thereby create necessary employment.
One must note that under the provisions of this proposed amendment the government's indirect contribution to approved construction projects would fall far short of the eighty per cent of the total contribution to this object, since a great many donations will be made to such projects by individuals whose income tax would not reach an eighty per cent rate.
He concludes by making a suggestion, a most constructive one, in the following paragraph:
The sponsors of this memorandum believe the proposal should be given serious consideration by the government on the grounds that the carrying out of construction projects would involve beneficially every province of the dominion. If the government does not see the necessity to pass the suggested amendment to the income tax enactment, then the government
is requested to make provision for authorizing the completion of construction projects which have already been started and for which funds have been solicited and partially collected.
That is a sensible proposal by the archbishop, on behalf of Protestant bodies, and it includes a proposal by the able Roman Catholic Bishop of London. Many other members of the clergy have made the same suggestion to the government.
We must consider what the universities in this country" have done. I do not know what the universities are going to do after the war. They are carrying on extensive scientific work, to which the university of Toronto has made a fine contribution, and all universities have in the war given all their buildings for war to the government. Let us look at the work the universities have done in the fields of science and medicine. I referred the other night to the progress science had made, and the glorious contribution made by science in this war and in the past twenty-five years has won the admiration- of the whole civilized world. We think at once of the Banting institute, the magnificent Toronto General hospital. We think of the work which the university of Toronto and all the other universities alike are doing in this war. and what science is doing. We think of the material progress being made as a result in trade and commerce, a progress which is most commendable.
In my view it is the duty of the government to come to the help of the universities and charities, at least to the extent suggested by the bishop. This was a most constructive suggestion, and he has performed a great national patriotic duty in making it.

The application of
resolution 32, and its effect upon universities, has been discussed in this debate. I would call the attention of the minister to a statement I made in the house on June 22, in which I pointed out the basic needs of education across the country, and the extent to which the federal government should come to the assistance of education I gave some details as to how that assistance should be apportioned. On the subject of university education I said:
The financial condition of our universities has been difficult; during the past years they have found it necessary to increase student fees. The fee required to be paid by a university student to-day is on the average, in all our Canadian universities, eighty per cent higher than it was ten years ago. As a result our universities are rapidly becoming institutions for the privileged class. The test of admission to our universities is rapidly becoming a means test rather than a test of ability. This trendy apart altogether from the inequity to the individual and the loss to society through the failure to train our ablest
Income War Tax

and brightest young people, can have but one effect on our universities; that is, a general impairment of educational standards. To-day our universities are operating on approximately $20,000,000. It is estimated that a federal grant of $5,000,000 would enable them to put their financial affairs in order and considerably reduce student fees.
As suggested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, I think in the first place the legislation which provided tax exemption to individuals and firms contributing to educational and charitable institutions was basically wrong. I am in agreement with the hon. member to the extent that at the present time some public funds should be made available at least to our universities, and also to other educational institutions.
To my mind the only sound way in which that could be done is by definite government grants for that purpose. I think the principle of permitting universities to go out and canvass corporations, with a view to inducing them to put their money into universities, instead of paying it in taxes, is basically wrong. It is the Canadian public which, in the final analysis, is making that payment; and in my view the payment should go directly to the institutions concerned. There is only one ground upon which I would support that principle, and that is if the government finds it constitutionally impossible to make a direct grant to educational institutions. If that were the case, then we might overcome that constitutional difficulty by the indirect or roundabout method of granting exemptions from taxation, until such time as the government can make direct contributions to such institutions.
Certainly the time has come when the federal government must face up to the educational means of this country. The federal government must come to realize that education can never be adequate in many of our provinces, not only in universities but in the lower schools, until federal support is forthcoming. I sincerely hope that in the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference some discussion will be had on that problem, and some effort made to bring about cooperation between the dominion government and the provincial legislature, without infringing upon their constitutional rights, so as to make it possible for the provinces to place their educational institutions on a better basis. In that way we could have education available to all the youth in this country who have the ability and the desire to attend such institutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In his speech on the budget the hon. member for York-Sunbury made a vigorous attack on the government's position in regard to charitable contributions. I did

not answer it during the debate, because I thought I would leave such discussion until the resolutions were reached. That resolution is now before the committee, and I should like now to give hon. members a brief resume of the steps taken, and the reasons for taking those steps.
Up until the 100 per cent excess profits tax was imposed

and it dated from July 1, 1942 -corporations made odd contributions for charitable purposes. Some corporations were fairly consistent givers, but not in very large sums. I suppose they felt they must always be in a position to justify to their shareholders the amounts of their contributions, and they were able to do that if the amounts were not excessive.
Up to a certain stage-I forget the year- corporations were given the same privileges as individuals. That ie, they had the privilege of deducting, for taxation purposes, charitable contributions up to ten per cent of the income. But there came a year-either 1941 or 1942- when we thought that should be reduced to five per cent; for, since corporate profits before taxation have increased enormously during the war, after taxation they have increased very little. Five per cent of the total corporate income was a very large sum, in the aggregate. Nevertheless, as the matter appeared to us at the time, we felt that they should be at liberty to contribute for charitable purposes up to five per cent of their income.
I am not altogether sure that the hon. member for York South is wrong in his statement that the whole principle is bad, but I am not sure that he is right. I certainly would not have been worried about the extent of contributions by corporate taxpayers to charities if it had not started to get manifestly excessive and away beyond any legitimate corporate purposes.
When we talk about charitable organizations we must remember that they go far beyond universities. They include a wide range of non-profit enterprises, such as churches and municipal projects of one kind and another. When this fever reached its height about January last I began to hear of municipal projects which were contemplated, some to the extent of 8500,000, 81,000,000 or $1,500,000, to be sponsored directly -or indirectly by the municipal authorities and to be financed by corporations in the municipalities. These. corporations had the privilege of deducting for taxation purposes up to five per cent of their income when donated for charitable purposes. If the company was paying 100 per cent excess profits taxes that meant that for the time being the whole 100 per cent would be diverted from the dominion treasury.

I am not saying that they were public funds, but otherwise they would be public funds. It meant that Canadian corporations were assuming the responsibility of diverting what would otherwise be public funds to charitable purposes of their own choice.
There was no possibility of getting an equitable geographical distribution of these donations; it was a haphazard method of diverting public funds and it was growing with tremendous rapidity. I was much concerned about it, because I knew how unpleasant a step it wou-ld be for the government to interfere with them. It is a thankless task to say to any taxpayer that he shall not donate money for charitable purposes. However, as the guardian of the treasury, as the custodian, to a certain extent at least, of public funds, I felt that the situation had reached the point where I should do something to stop it from going on any longer. I heard of campaigns which were planned and which were being planned in various parts of Canada. On one occasion I was consulted about a campaign that was projected.
It became fashionable, shall I say, for canvassers to go to corporate taxpayers and say frankly to them, "The government will get this if you do not let us have it; why not give it to us?" I do not think we could object to that type of canvass, but it always irked me to have canvasses like that made. I do not like it in time of war, no matter how fine the charitable project may be. It was something that went against my grain, but I do not think I could have taken any exception to it so long as our law was what it was. They could very well say, "There is your statute; that is what parliament has done; you cannot blame us for taking advantage of it, and we will pass upon the patriotism and the ethics of our course."
I felt that the only thing to do was to make a statement, which I did on January 31. This statement would have to take effect at once because no advance notice could be given. To have given advance notice would have meant the feverish collection of donations in the next few days, and I felt I had to make a statement, which I did at the end of
January, with regard to donations made after January 31, indicating that there would be restrictions. I had no power to do this as Minister of Finance; the government had no power to do it, but I could give notice that when the budget was brought down I would introduce legislation which would be effective as from February 1, and that is what I am doing.
You scared them.

Those were the ones being subjected to this intensive canvass by persons interested in various charitable projects.

It was contended that they should not be denied the full tax advantage if they kept within those limits, that they should not be penalized for doing what they had done before the 100 per cent excess profits tax came in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree that that would be unfair to the taxpayer, but I think it would be unfair to the crown if it were spread over the expectancy of life, and for this reason: If the taxpayer lives for longer than his expectancy of life the crown would be collecting taxes only for the period of his life expectancy. If the taxpayer lives for a shorter period than his expectancy of life, the crown would be collecting taxes only on part of the years. If we knew exactly how many years each employee would live I do not know that there would be anything unjust about spreading the payment over that number of years, but to take the expectancy of life as a basis would be far more unfavourable to the crown than that would be. Therefore I think it is fair to take a period somewhat shorter than the normal expectancy of life. Five years is shorter than the average expectancy of life at sixty or even at seventy.
Of course it would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nevertheless I do not believe that there is any essential justice in taking the expectancy of life, because in all those cases where a person dies before that period runs out, the crown collects income tax only on part of the amount and, when they live beyond the expectancy of life, the crown is limited to taxes on the exact amount.

It is a matter of equity; it cannot be exact. But surely in equity the subject has some rights as well as the crown. Supposing a man who has been working for a company which did not have a superannuation plan gets a lump sum gratuity at sixty. It is true that these superannuation plans are becoming more the vogue, as they should be, but a great many of our companies have not had them up to date. Suppose that an

Income War Tax
employee or executive on retirement at sixty is given a lump sum of $5,000 or $25,000; he will be taxed on one-fifth of that sum in each of the next succeeding five years, which is a very heavy tax, almost an extortionate tax at the present high rates. JBut suppose his expectancy of life was fifteen years. Why could we not compromise and spread the taxation over ten years? Surely that would be working against the subject and in favour of the crown. But when the minister takes an arbitrary figure of five years he is making the principle work against the subject to a degree which is against all principles of equity.
Some of these large corporations retire all their executives at sixty in order to bring in new blood and give an opportunity to the younger men. We have seen the same principle adopted in the air force. The minister for air has stated in the house that rapid promotion in the air force brings its own penalty, because when men were rapidly promoted they were got rid of at a comparative early age to make room for younger officers who had won their spurs on the field and these younger men were to be promoted to the senior jobs. The same thing applies in business. The Woolworth company retires all its executives at sixty, I believe, to make room for younger men coming in with fresh ideas. Suppose a man is given a substantial sum upon retirement from such a company at sixty, and he has a life expectancy of from fifteen to twenty years. Under this clause he is going to have taxed away the greater part of that capital sum in a five-year period, and it will go to the crown instead of being used for the purpose for which it was given to the employee. I hope that the minister, who surely seeks only fairness in this regard, will see fit to arrive at something that will be in favour of the crown, if you like-I have no objection to that-but that will also be fair to the subject. If we adopted the principle of life expectancy, less a few years, if you will, it would give equity to the subject as well as making sure that the crown gets all the revenue to which it is entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just how far should parliament go in arranging the affairs of taxpayers for them?. This is a matter which is entirely in the hands of the employer and the employee. If the employer wishes to pay the employee an annuity or pension, there is nothing to prevent the employee from accepting it, in which event the employee will be taxed each year as long as he lives. If the employer wishes to spread it over ten years, or over seven or eight years all that can be arranged between themselves and the taxation
imposed accordingly. If they wish to make another arrangement, to give a lump sum gratuity, there is no presumption that that gratuity is intended to be spread over the remaining years of the employee's life.
That is a reasonable presumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no more presumption that it is to be spread over the remaining years of his life than over the next five years. So that all we can do is to take an arbitrary figure and just say that if you want to arrange your affairs in that way and take a lump sum we will not tax it all in one year, which is the law at the present time, but will spread it over five years;- and if you want it in smaller sums, arrange accordingly to pay it in smaller sums.

Of course a corporation could use its head, if you will, and give a life annuity to the employee. There are cases. How they arise or why, I am not in a position to say; but the very fact that the minister brings in this resolution shows that there are cases where men and women, former employees of companies, do get lump sums given them. The minister can say better than I can why they get them, but he has pointed out that if the company would use its head and give the employees an annual income in place of a lump sum the government would get only so much taxation. On the other hand, because they happen to have given a lump sum, for reasons which the minister can explain better than I can, the taxation is not only three or four times but eight or ten times as much as it otherwise would be. The crown wishes to take advantage of the subject's lack of knowledge of the taxation laws of the country. I am only pleading for something approximating the taxation that the crown would get if the company used its head.
Exactly the same question came up last year in connection with annuities. There, if the husband seeking to provide for his widow leaves an annuity, constituted of all the principal he has, we find that the widow pays three or four times as much taxation as if the widow received the capital outright. The hon. member for Vancouver East supported me after he had heard the arguments and changed his mind against the minister. This case is similar to the annuity question. If a man knew exactly how long his widow would live he would say to her, " Here is a capital sum to draw an income from during your normal expectancy of life, of fifteen or twenty years, and you will also take $400 or $500 of capital and you will have enough to get by on." But

ht does not know how long she will live, and because he does the only sensible thing he can do and buys her an annuity, the government collects four or five times as much as it otherwise would^
This case is similar in principle. I admit that if the companies used their heads the crown would not get this excessive taxation, to which it is not entitled. At any rate, the cases are there, and I only ask that the subject, seeing that he does not know the incidence of the taxation laws of the country, should be fairly dealt with. I submit that some clause should be framed having as its basis the normal expectation of life of the person who receives a lump sum on retirement. Normally I should say, as the minister has admitted, that if a man retires at sixty or seventy his expectancy is ten years. But the crown wishes to have all the money it can get even from poor people who are trying to provide for their old age and it fixes the period at five years. Ten is not too large a figure, and I should be glad to move that the word five be changed to ten in the section. It is only an approximation. It does not go the whole way, but it does come a little nearer to what is fair and it does not rob the treasury of anything to which it is rightfully entitled.

To-day the prospector employs a great deal of scientific equipment. He uses a diamond drill, and a process of radio-location known as the doodlebug. He employs a great many scientific instruments, and has to be trained in his work. Not only that, but in the main ore-bearing belts in Ontario and Quebec he has to overcome a great deal of overburden, and has to get down to bed rock.
In other words, he has to do a great deal of work that the old prospector, the man who went out and found the minerals showing, did not have to do. His work to-day is entirely different. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This proposed resolution covers really what is a technical point. At
the present time our Excess Profits Tax Act defines standard profits, and I quote:
The average yearly profits of a taxpayer in the standard period in carrying out what was in the opinion of the minister the same class of business as the business of the taxpayer in the year of taxation.
The proposed amendment provides for the determination of standard profits by the board of referees where the business of the taxpayer is substantially different from the business carried on by the taxpayer in the standard period. In the act there is no definition of standard profits where the business is substantially unlike the business carried on during the standard period,

Excess Profits Tax
and there is no power to send to the board of referees.	In other words, to give an
example, the business may have been carried on during the standard period to manufacture stoves, and by reason of shortage of material or something else they switched to the manufacture of a completely different commodity. There is a gap in the act. Under those circumstances it can be argued that they have no standard profits at all because they are not carrying on the same class of business. I would say it is a technical point arising out of the definition contained in the act. It does not enlarge the scope of the act in any way. It just covers one of those drafting oversights, and probably on balance it may be and should be beneficial to the taxpayer.

Suppose the stove manufacturer had a fairly successful business and had a reasonable return on his capital over and above what the board of referees are allowed to grant. Owing to shortage of materials the stove business is no longer in operation and the owner turns his equipment over to the manufacture of shells. It is clear he cannot use his old manufacturing base. What I want to find out is what authority the board of referees have to grant him a base over and above five to seven per cent, is it, on his assets in connection with the manufacture of shells, which may be very small in relation to his pre-war profits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The section which defines standard profits is paragraph (i) of section 2 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, which reads:
Standard profits means the average yearly profits of the taxpayer in the standard period in carrying on what was in the opinion of the minister the same class of business as the business of the taxpayer in the year of taxation or the standard profits ascertained in accordance with section 5 of this act.
It could be argued that in the case such as has been cited the taxpayer has no standard profits at all and that, therefore, all his profits are excess profits. Or it might be argued that since he has no standard profits he is not subject to the provisions of the Excess Profits Tax Act at all and is only subject to the Income War Tax Act. It is to clarify that position and to provide that in the case of a taxpayer whose business is substantially different from the class of business which he carried on during the base period the question of his standard profits shall be referred to the board of referees for determination. Of course, the board of referees will be governed by the general rules respecting determination of standard profits.

It may easily turn out that if the stove manufacturer was making
$100,000 taxable profits before the war and has turned his business entirely over to war production, on a strict evaluation of his assets in that class of business the board of referees would only grant him perhaps $10,000 or $15,000. Is that a situation which might arise out of the application of this resolution? It seems rigorous. I cannot see that the direction of the board of referees is such as to allow a fair return commensurate with what he was earning before.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He will have the same rights as every other taxpayer appearing before the board of referees. First, as to new business, the standard is determined by the board of referees in accordance with the rules laid down by the act. If he can show that he has a depressed business, then he would get standard profits determined under section 5. If he can show that the business was one in which capital was not a major factor, then the board' of referees can take that into account. But, broadly speaking, where the business is substantially different from the business carried on during the standard period, the standard profit is to be determined by the board of referees.

7.	That the provision permitting a taxpayer to -deduct from tax. the amount paid to any foreign country for income tax in respect of the income of the taxpayer from sources therein, be amended by deleting the requirement that such foreign country in imposing tax allow a similar credit to persons in respect of income thereof from sources within Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the parliamentary assistant explain this resolution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This resolution corresponds exactly to resolution 25 of the income tax resolutions which were discussed at some length this morning. It is exactly the same provision. If a Canadian income taxpayer is subject to tax abroad he may deduct from his Canadian tax the amount of tax which he is obliged to pay in the foreign jurisdiction. That is the law now. But the requirement that the foreign country should afford a similar privilege to our citizens is now being eliminated, and the Canadian taxpayer can take that credit whether the foreign country grants a reciprocal provision or not. It is exactly the same provision that was set out in resolution 35 with respect to income tax, as distinct from the excess profits tax.

Which other countries do not afford us reciprocal provisions? I presume the only two countries in which we are interested are Great Britain and the United States.
Excess Profits Tax

Possibly there are some others, but the minister might explain why we cannot get reciprocal provisions with them and what countries they are.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

The deputy minister advises me that in the department they have a list, which may be incomplete, setting out the various statutory provisions, but that is not here. Certainly the United States and Great Britain do have this reciprocal arrangement, and they are the two most important countries from our point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I listened closely to the minister's arguments in favour of this move, which he gave on June 26, and I have reread them as they appear at page 4182 of Hansard. I grant that the minister has made a case for the step he is taking, but I consider that some of the things that strike me in this connection should be pointed out. I am prepared to have the minister correct me if my understanding is not accurate. It seems to me that once this upward adjustment of standard profits is allowed, it must be admitted that it will have certain effects. It will provide some relief in taxation to certain corporations. It

will result in some loss of revenue to the treasury. It will also result in certain increased profits to corporations and, to the extent that there may be greater profits for distribution in the form of dividends, it has a bearing on the fight against inflation. As I have said, I grant that the minister has made a case, but the point I wish to emphasize is that if he finds it necessary to take this step, in spite of the results I have enumerated, he should appreciate the position when some of the rest of us in this house come along and suggest adjustments that we feel need to be made, even though they may have some of these same effects. The parliamentary assistant and I had a little spat the other day over that very attitude.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Very friendly, though.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Oh, quite; the fyon.
gentleman and I get along very well even when we fight. The point I was making then was that the adjustments for which we on this side of the house ask should be considered in the same light as the adjustments proposed by the government. I suggest that resolution 8 is a particular example of an adjustment the minister has found necessary, despite the effects which I have enumerated as likely to result. I have in mind at the moment one group of people in particular who are much concerned at the delay in making an adjustment as far as they are concerned; I refer to the railroad employees throughout the country. For some considerable time their case has been before one of the boards, and they have been anxiously awaiting a decision. The discussion that has gone on in the press in regard to that matter has related to the very things I have mentioned, particularly, the fight against inflation. Still these things are allowed to happen in this case, while on the other hand we have the railroad employees who are feeling quite disturbed at the long delay in dealing with their case. I know that does not come directly under the minister, but it is part of the government's wage-freezing and anti-inflation policy. The point I am suggesting here is that there has been some relaxation in resolution 8 as far as the profits of private corporations are concerned. We ask for similar consideration for other groups of people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is a pretty farfetched comparison. The idea of the Excess Profits Tax Act is to take away excess profits; but when a company grows into an altogether different sort of thing than it was in the standard period; when it becomes a much larger entity than it was in the standard period, then the provision is no longer fair.

I grant that, but the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is saying that he wants fairness, and so do I. He points to certain things and says that this has some inflationary effect. It would be very remote indeed, I should think. We would have to take a particular case and trace it through. It does have this effect, I admit: If you raise the standard profits it makes a little less than you take away in 100 per cent profit, but whether or not that would have any effect upon dividends I should think would be very uncertain.
