speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No, I am just trying to emphasize the fact that if the reason for this is the ground of fairness, that is likewise the ground we use in the cases vre bring to the attention of the minister.

I would point out to the hon. member that this is not an increase in rates earned. It is simply an application of the same rate to a greater number of employees. There is no increase in the rate. It is simply that more capital has been put into it, and they are getting returns on it for the first time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is a relief in taxation, as compared with what the case would be if the resolution were not passed.

It is a relief from a hardship. At the same time, the second amendment means that if the amount of capital is less than it was before, he ought not to be allowed to earn so much. The rate remains the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If you let the situation alone you would be taking more than 100 per cent of the true excess. It is merely applying the 100 per cent rule on a fair basis. That is all it is doing. It is necessary to do certain things in a time of war that are not altogether fair, because of the terrible consequences of not taking that course of action. The economy becomes so complicated that precise equity in every instance is impossible. I presume there is not precise equity here even yet. Certainly there has been inequity through the year.
This is applicable to 1944 for the first time, even though the company had been growing during that period. There were inequalities all during that time, and they were not recognized at all. But there comes a time when
it becomes a little too difficult, and an adjustment has to be made.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to some of the remarks I made in my budget speech. I made a plea for a step-up for those in the salaried brackets, above those who received cost of living bonus. As I said at that time, many people accept low salaries in their early years, just as do civil servants, until they reach a maximum. Owing to the effect of the wage-freezing order their wages have been kept at a very low level. I believe it is three or four years-perhaps three years is correct-since the wage-freezing order was made. So that I think consideration should be given to the effect which that order has had on many of the white-collared class who not only have been faced with higher taxes-as we all have-but are not getting the advances which they otherwise would have got, and who as a result are feeling a peculiar hardship.
Wage-earners, particularly those who are unionized, have been able to get increases in wages or, in some cases, have transferred their employment. But many of our finest citizens, receiving small salaries, people in the white-collared class, have had no increases in pay, yet their responsibilities have greatly increased during that time. It seems to me that there must come a time-and I think that time has already come-when consideration should be given to a step-up in their salaries, where justified, and where employers would be willing to make the increase which would ordinarily be made, if the freezing order had not been in force.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I listened to the hon. member attentively when he made his budget speech. It is a question whether there should be a gradual retreat.
When a man becomes more useful to his employer, it is just like an increase in capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say anything in reply to those representations. The trouble is they are there on every side. They are on prices, they are on wages, they are on salaries and on everything else. I do not know what the government should do under those circumstances. You might very easily make a retreat, and then the fight against inflation would become a rout. I might easily do that. But, on the other hand, certain adjustments have to be made from time to time. As the hon. member has said, there have been a great many wage adjustments.

9.	That companies which elect or have elected since January 1, 1940, under the Income War Tax Act to file consolidated returns be not permitted to file such returns under the Excess Profits Tax Act in respect of fiscal periods ending on or after January 1, 1944.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May we have an
explanation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to explain it. The law now permits companies which have wholly-owned subsidiaries to file a consolidated tax return, upon paying two per cent additional tax, I believe it is. Up to comparatively recently, in the case of a company and its subsidiaries, the standard profit for excess profits tax was taken as being the standard profit of the parent, together with the standard profit of the subsidiaries.
A ruling was issued some time ago that in the case of companies which had elected to consolidate subsequently to January 1, 1940, the standard profit should be restricted to the largest standard profit of a company in the group, plus $5,000 for each of the other companies.
This measure further restricts that right, and it provides that in the case of companies which elected prior to January 1, 1940, to consolidate, there is no change in their position. That was before the war. In the case of companies which have elected since that time, after January 1, 1944, they will no longer be able to file consolidated returns for purposes of excess profits tax. It is a measure which I think would have the effect of curbing or checking possible abuses. In other words, each company will stand on its own feet so far as excess profits tax and standard profits are concerned.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act, and to provide:-
1. That the definition of "child" be extended to include that child to whom the deceased stands in loco parentis.

Under this act as it stands
at the present time an estate is taxed in accordance with the terms of the will, but in some provinces there is what is known as a testator's family maintenance act under which judges of the superior courts have the power to vary the succession. I understand that the Dominion Succession Duty Act pays no attention to an order made under one of these provincial acts, and the result is that succession duty may be levied against a person, say on $10,000, when a judge of the provincial court may order that that person shall receive only $1,000. I understand that some cases have been adjusted by refunds of money or something of that sort, or by the passing of a special order, but I think the act should be amended so that situations of this kind will not arise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am totally unaware of the situation to which the hon. gentleman refers, and I shall have to give it consideration between now and the time the bill is brought in. I shall have to take it up with the Department of National Revenue to see if consideration has been given to the problem. The deputy minister informs me that he does not know of the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will look into the matter. On the facts stated it would look as though the taxpayer should have a refund, but I do not know.

I understand that this act was passed to raise additional money during war time. It is purely a succession duty proposition, but there is one thing I should like to point out and object strenuously against. The people who administer the Dominion Succession Duty Act are the same officials who look after the collection of the dominion income tax. They use the powers granted to them to prevent the issuance of a certificate in order to force the representative of the estate or the beneficiaries to file income tax returns over a period of years in the event that they have not been filed.
I suggest that the administration is taking an unfair advantage of the Dominion Succession Duty Act to go into another field of taxation in order to hold up a person from getting a little bit of money. I have a recent case where the only asset of the estate was a little bit of insurance. The widow knew nothing about her husband's affairs, but she was obliged to dig around for a lot of information about her husband's business in order to be able to file income tax returns for a number of years before his death. I do not contend that the deceased was justified in not filing income tax returns, but the fact is that this money was held up and the certificate was not issued. The powers granted under this act are being used for an entirely different purpose. I suggest that if the matter is to be dealt with, it should be dealt with under the Income War Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We were not taking unfair advantage at all. After all, the estate was being wound up, and it is the duty of the taxing officials to see that any income tax returns should be filed that have not been filed. It is their duty to do this when the size of the estate indicates that returns should have been filed.

The estate may indicate that a man was fairly well equipped financially, but this case was a small estate of about $5,000 life insurance. It happened to be the only cash asset the widow had, but it was held up until she furnished income tax statements with respect to the last three or four years before her husband's death.

2. That when a person is given a general power of appointment or disposal over property, such property be subject to duty as if it were given directly to him, and, upon his death, the person then benefiting be regarded as his successor for purposes of taxation.

I should like to mention a specific case which I think will come under this resolution. Since this case is public property I will mention the name. It is the Arthur E. Burgett estate. Mr. Burgett was the former bishop of Edmonton and his estate was left entirely to charity. I should like to show what happened to the estate. The deceased resided at Oak Bay, Victoria, British Columbia, and he died on December 13, 1942. He was formerly Bishop of the Diocese of Edmonton, but resigned his episcopal office in 1940 and removed his place of residence to Victoria. He was unmarried and had no relatives in this country.
His estate had an inventory value of $179,469 and consisted almost entirely of securities which were in his possession in Victoria. By his will be made provision for an old servant by the devise of a cottage and the bequest of an annuity. The total amount expended for the benefit of this servant was between $14,000 and $15,000. The point I wish to bring up is in connection with the residue of his estate. This amounted to $163,914, and apart from a small bequest to the Diocese of Edmonton, it was given for the aid of divinity students at Bishop's college, Lennoxville, Quebec, and Trinity college, Toronto, and for missionary work in the ecclesiastical province of Rupert's Land.

Succession Duty

made any allowance for duties paid in other jurisdictions in estimating the taxation rate which was fixed on the aggregate value of the estate everywhere.
It seems to me an indefensible policy that there should be so many jurisdictions in this case, and I bring this matter up on this resolution just to show what is happening to-day through our system of dual and triple taxation by succession duties. The whole estate of this bishop with the exception of a small bequest to a faithful servant was left to charity, and yet very nearly fifty thousand dollars in taxation was imposed. I wonder whether the committee is aware that this is the sort of duties that are being imposed to-day by our succession duty acts. Practically the whole estate was given to charity. I hope the minister agrees with me that these rates are quite indefensible in justice and in law. This estate is closed now and has been probated1, but I honestly suggest that the minister give serious consideration to an immediate conference with the provinces, so that these double and triple imposts shall not continue to destroy particularly assets of a clergyman of the church who was leaving his entire fortune to charity. I think our whole succession duty system should be given the most careful revision to prevent things like this from happening in the future.

speechtext: I have not anything really to say about that. It is not strictly relevant to the resolution.
